data.title: Diagnostic and prognostic significance of neurofilament light chain NF-L, but not progranulin and S100B, in the course of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis: Data from the German MND-net.
data.abstract: There is a need for diagnostic, prognostic, and monitoring blood biomarkers for ALS. We aimed to analyse and compare proposed candidate markers for disease progression in the course of ALS. Blood samples were taken from 125 ALS patients, including nine patients with C9orf72 or SOD1 mutation, at regular intervals of six months. ALS patients were characterized by the ALS functional rating scale (ALSFRS-R) and the Edinburgh Cognitive and Behavioural ALS Screen (ECAS). We quantified neurofilament light chain (NF-L), S100B, and progranulin (PGRN) and analysed it in relation to disease progression. Results showed that, at baseline, serum concentrations of NF-L but not PGRN or S100B discriminated significantly between ALS and controls. Within 24 months follow-up the marker concentrations remained stable. Baseline serum NF-L levels correlated with survival time, which was confirmed in subgroups with fast, intermediate, and slow disease progression and there was a weak association with disease duration. For S100B and PGRN we found an association with ALSFRS-R score changes and a trend for decreased levels in the fast progressor subgroup. In conclusion, serum NF-L in any ALS disease stage is a promising marker to support diagnosis and predict outcome, while serum PGRN and S100B are only of minor prognostic value.

data.title: Serum asymmetric dimethylarginine level correlates with the progression and prognosis of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE
The aim was to investigate the association between serum asymmetric dimethylarginine (ADMA) levels and the progression and prognosis of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), and to compare cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and serum ADMA levels with other biomarkers of ALS.
METHODS
Serum ADMA levels of sporadic ALS patients (n = 68), disease control patients (n = 54) and healthy controls (n = 20) were measured using liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry. Correlations of the ADMA level and other markers (nitric oxide and neurofilament light chain levels) were analyzed. Changes in the ALS Functional Rating Scale Revised (ALSFRS-R) score from the onset of disease (ALSFRS-R pre-slope) was used to assess disease progression. Survival was evaluated using the Cox proportional hazards model and Kaplan-Meier analysis.
RESULTS
The serum ADMA level was substantially higher in patients with ALS than in healthy controls and disease controls. Serum ADMA level correlated with CSF ADMA level (r = 0.591, p < 0.0001) and was independently associated with the ALSFRS-R pre-slope (r = 0.505, p < 0.0001). Patients with higher serum ADMA levels had less favorable prognoses. CSF ADMA level significantly correlated with CSF neurofilament light chain level (r = 0.456, p = 0.0002) but not with nitric oxide level (r = 0.194, p = 0.219).
CONCLUSION
Serum ADMA level is an independent biomarker of ALS disease progression and prognosis and reflects the degree of motor neuron degeneration.

# Summary

Neurofilament light chain (NfL) is a sensitive marker of axonal damage in ALS, measurable in serum and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), and consistently associates with both survival and the rate of functional decline across disease stages. Higher levels at diagnosis predict shorter survival and faster ALSFRS-R deterioration, and in several cohorts this prognostic signal is independent of clinical factors. Complementary markers can refine risk stratification, particularly in advanced disease, and CSF neurofilaments show concordant prognostic patterns with serum NfL.

# Serum NfL: Survival and Functional Decline

Prospective data show that serum NfL at diagnosis is markedly elevated in ALS versus controls and is associated with shorter survival, with Kaplan–Meier analyses reporting hazard ratios around 4.4–5.4 per unit increase and 40–50% 50-week survival below prognostic cutoffs, declining near zero above cutoffs. In multivariable Cox models, serum NfL, weight loss, and site of onset are independent predictors of death, and similar independence is observed when restricting to patients with pulmonary function measures, supporting robust prognostic value early in disease course. <cite id="40009787">Serum NfL shows high diagnostic and prognostic accuracy in ALS, with hazard ratios of 4.4–5.4 and 40%–50% 50-week survival below prognostic cutoffs, and proposed diagnostic/prognostic thresholds</cite> <cite id="31437330">Serum NfL, weight loss, and site at onset are independent predictors of death in ALS, and sNfL also independently predicts death when restricted to patients with spirometry data</cite>.

Longitudinal analyses link serum NfL to the rate of ALSFRS-R decline; in a subgroup with repeated ALSFRS-R scores, sNfL positively correlated with the decline rate (r = 0.571, P < 10^-12), indicating that higher NfL tracks faster functional deterioration. <cite id="31437330">Serum NfL positively correlates with ALSFRS-R rate of decline (r = 0.571, P < 10^-12)</cite>. In larger cohorts, serum NfL increases with advancing disease stage and correlates with progression rate, while also discriminating rapidly versus slowly progressive ALS, reinforcing its value across the disease continuum. <cite id="40705135">Serum NfL is elevated in ALS versus controls (AUC 0.969), increases with advancing King's stage (τ = 0.226, p = 0.011), and correlates with disease progression rate (r = 0.309, p = 0.001)</cite> <cite id="39666115">Across 270 ALS patients, higher serum NfL was associated with higher mortality risk at 6 months, 1 year, and 3 years, and integrated analyses identified distinct functional decline trajectories</cite>.

# CSF NfL and Related Neurofilaments: Survival and Decline

CSF neurofilament markers are also elevated in ALS and show prognostic concordance with serum NfL. In a large cohort, CSF NfL, NfM, and pNfH distinguished ALS from mimics and healthy controls, and higher CSF neurofilament levels aligned with faster ALSFRS-R progression at baseline and longitudinally, with AUCs of 0.78–0.85 for classifying fast versus slow progressors. Importantly, lower CSF neurofilament levels corresponded to higher survival probability, mirroring serum findings. <cite id="39575564">CSF NfM, NfL, and pNfH were elevated in ALS; higher CSF NfM predicted faster progression (fast vs slow) and all three markers showed comparable performance (AUCs 0.78–0.85), with higher survival probability for patients with low CSF levels</cite>.

Earlier work similarly found that CSF and serum NFL and pNFH were significantly increased in ALS, correlated negatively with ALSFRS-R and disease duration, positively with progression rate and UMN scores, and independently predicted survival in Cox models, supporting their use as biomarkers of disease burden and outcome. <cite id="34866307">Serum and CSF NFL and pNFH were significantly increased in ALS, negatively correlated with ALSFRS-R and disease duration, positively with progression rate and UMN score, and independently predicted survival in Cox regression</cite> <cite id="27819158">Baseline serum NF-L discriminated ALS from controls and correlated with survival time across subgroups defined by progression speed, while PGRN and S100B had limited prognostic value</cite>.

# Stage-Dependent Insights and Complementary Markers

NfL signals are present from diagnosis and strengthen as disease advances, paralleling worsening functional status and survival risk. <cite id="40705135">Serum NfL increases with King's stage and correlates with progression rate</cite> <cite id="39666115">Higher serum NfL associates with higher mortality risk across 6-, 1-, and 3-year horizons</cite>. In late-stage ALS (King's stage III–IV), glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) adds independent prognostic value, with elevated GFAP associated with markedly poorer survival (HR 6.907, 95% CI 1.978–24.119), suggesting distinct cellular contributors alongside ongoing axonal damage. <cite id="40705135">Elevated CSF GFAP was independently associated with poorer survival in advanced ALS (King's stage 3–4), with a hazard ratio of 6.907 (95% CI: 1.978–24.119)</cite>. Combinations of NfL with other markers (e.g., MCP-1 or GFAP) can improve survival prediction accuracy, supporting biomarker panels over single markers. <cite id="39915090">Plasma miR-214 correlated with NfL and MCP-1 and improved survival prediction when combined with NfL</cite>.

Converging evidence from metabolic markers also aligns with neurodegeneration readouts: serum and CSF ADMA, which correlates with CSF NfL, independently predicts worse ALSFRS-R slope and shorter survival, reinforcing the link between neuronal injury and functional decline. <cite id="35128793">Serum ADMA was higher in ALS, correlated with CSF ADMA and CSF NfL, and independently associated with ALSFRS-R pre-slope and survival</cite>.

# Practical Implications

- Early disease: At diagnosis, serum NfL provides independent prognostic information alongside age, site of onset, and respiratory/functional measures; higher levels indicate substantially higher mortality risk and faster ALSFRS-R decline, enabling risk stratification and counseling. <cite id="31437330">Serum NfL, weight loss, and site at onset are independent predictors of death; higher sNfL corresponds to faster decline</cite> <cite id="40009787">Cutoff-based survival probabilities show 40%–50% 50-week survival below thresholds, dropping near zero above</cite>.
- Disease progression monitoring: Serial NfL measurements track worsening neurodegeneration; elevated and rising levels suggest accelerated decline and may justify more aggressive supportive or interventional strategies. <cite id="31437330">sNfL correlates with ALSFRS-R rate of decline</cite> <cite id="40705135">NfL correlates with progression rate and increases with stage</cite>.
- Advanced disease: In stages III–IV, adding GFAP to NfL can refine prognosis, reflecting evolving glial pathology alongside axonal injury. <cite id="40705135">GFAP independently predicts poorer survival in advanced ALS</cite>.
- CSF vs serum: CSF neurofilaments show parallel prognostic associations—elevated levels predict shorter survival and faster decline, and lower CSF neurofilaments confer better survival—supporting their use when serum collection is impractical or when higher specificity is desired. <cite id="39575564">Lower CSF neurofilament levels correspond to higher survival; CSF markers classify fast vs slow progressors</cite> <cite id="34866307">CSF NFL and pNFH independently predict survival and correlate with ALSFRS-R and progression rate</cite>.

# Limitations and Considerations

- Confounders: Age, BMI, and comorbidities can correlate with NfL levels, and multivariable models are needed to isolate disease-specific effects. <cite id="40009787">NfL and GFAP levels were associated with age and BMI, considered confounders</cite>.
- Assay variability: Different platforms quantify NfL with high correlation, but thresholds and clinical cutoffs vary; harmonization and platform-specific interpretation are important. <cite id="40009787">High correlation across serum NfL platforms (R^2 = 0.939–0.963) and proposed cutoffs for diagnostic and prognostic use</cite>.
- Specificity: While NfL is a strong prognostic marker of neurodegeneration, its limited disease specificity argues for combining with markers like GFAP or inflammatory/cytokine readouts to improve stratification, particularly in later stages. <cite id="40705135">NfL remains robust for progression, GFAP adds independent prognostic value in advanced disease</cite> <cite id="39915090">Combining miR-214 with NfL or MCP-1 improved survival prediction</cite>.

# Bottom Line

Across serum and CSF, higher NfL levels at any stage are robustly associated with shorter survival and faster ALSFRS-R decline in ALS, with independent prognostic value in multivariable models. The prognostic signal is detectable early and strengthens with disease progression, and combining NfL with stage- and mechanism-specific markers (e.g., GFAP in advanced disease, inflammatory or metabolic markers) improves risk stratification and may guide individualized care. <cite id="31437330">Higher serum NfL predicts death independently and correlates with faster functional decline</cite> <cite id="40009787">Serum NfL cutoffs yield marked differences in 50-week survival probabilities</cite> <cite id="39575564">Lower CSF neurofilament levels correspond to higher survival; CSF markers classify fast vs slow progressors</cite> <cite id="34866307">CSF NFL and pNFH independently predict survival and track ALSFRS-R decline</cite> <cite id="40705135">NfL increases with stage and correlates with progression rate; GFAP adds prognostic value in advanced ALS</cite>.

<snippet id="35764364">Title: Tumor-targeted interleukin-12 synergizes with entinostat to overcome PD-1/PD-L1 blockade-resistant tumors harboring MHC-I and APM deficiencies.
Authors: Minnar, Christine M, Chariou, Paul L, Horn, Lucas A et al. | Year: 2022 | Journal: Journal for immunotherapy of cancer
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) has achieved unprecedented success in treating multiple cancer types. However, clinical benefit remains modest for most patients with solid malignancies due to primary or acquired resistance. Tumor-intrinsic loss of major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC-I) and aberrations in antigen processing machinery (APM) and interferon gamma (IFN-γ) pathways have been shown to play an important role in ICB resistance. While a plethora of combination treatments are being investigated to overcome ICB resistance, there are few identified preclinical models of solid tumors harboring these deficiencies to explore therapeutic interventions that can bypass ICB resistance. Here, we investigated the combination of the epigenetic modulator entinostat and the tumor-targeted immunocytokine NHS-IL12 in three different murine tumor models resistant to αPD-1/αPD-L1 (anti-programmed cell death protein 1/anti-programmed death ligand 1) and harboring MHC-I, APM, and IFN-γ response deficiencies and differing tumor mutational burden (TMB).
METHODS
Entinostat and NHS-IL12 were administered to mice bearing TC-1/a9 (lung, HPV16 E6/E7 + ), CMT.64 lung, or RVP3 sarcoma tumors. Antitumor efficacy and survival were monitored. Comprehensive tumor microenvironment (TME) and spleen analysis of immune cells, cytokines, and chemokines was performed. Additionally, whole transcriptomic analysis was carried out on TC-1/a9 tumors. Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) datasets were analyzed for translational relevance.
RESULTS
We demonstrate that the combination of entinostat and NHS-IL12 therapy elicits potent antitumor activity and survival benefit through prolonged activation and tumor infiltration of cytotoxic CD8 + T cells, across αPD-1/αPD-L1 refractory tumors irrespective of TMB, including in the IFN-γ signaling-impaired RVP3 tumor model. The combination therapy promoted M1-like macrophages and activated antigen-presenting cells while decreasing M2-like macrophages and regulatory T cells in a tumor-dependent manner. This was associated with increased levels of IFN-γ, IL-12, chemokine (C-X-C motif) ligand 9 (CXCL9), and CXCL13 in the TME. Further, the combination therapy synergized to promote MHC-I and APM upregulation, and enrichment of JAK/STAT (janus kinase/signal transducers and activators of transcription), IFN-γ-response and antigen processing-associated pathways. A biomarker signature of the mechanism involved in these studies is associated with patients' overall survival across multiple tumor types.
CONCLUSIONS
Our findings provide a rationale for combining the tumor-targeting NHS-IL12 with the histone deacetylase inhibitor entinostat in the clinical setting for patients unresponsive to αPD-1/αPD-L1 and/or with innate deficiencies in tumor MHC-I, APM expression, and IFN-γ signaling.</snippet>

# Summary

Across multiple tumor types treated with PD‑1/PD‑L1 inhibitors, the tumor-intrinsic mechanisms most consistently linked to primary resistance are defects in antigen presentation and interferon-γ (IFN-γ) signaling, including loss of MHC class I and more general antigen processing machinery (APM) pathway alterations. These defects blunt CD8+ T‑cell recognition and immune infiltration, producing a "cold," non‑inflamed tumor microenvironment that is poorly responsive to PD‑1/PD‑L1 blockade. Cross‑cancer analyses (e.g., TCGA) and preclinical models converge on these pathways, and combinations that restore antigen presentation and IFN-γ–responsive programs can re‑sensitize tumors to immunotherapy.

# Key Mechanisms and Evidence

- Antigen presentation defects: Loss of MHC‑I and mutations in antigen processing components (e.g., β2‑microglobulin, TAP, tapasin, ERAP) reduce presentation of tumor‑associated peptides to CD8+ T cells, undermining the main target of PD‑1/PD‑L1 pathway blockade. Preclinical models explicitly deficient in MHC‑I or APM components are refractory to anti‑PD‑1/anti‑PD‑L1, and restoring antigen presentation (e.g., with epigenetic modulators or immunocytokines) restores CD8+ T‑cell infiltration and antitumor activity across such models, including those with IFN‑γ pathway impairment, indicating this is a primary resistance axis across tumor types. <cite id="35764364">Tumor‑intrinsic loss of MHC‑I and aberrations in antigen processing machinery and interferon gamma pathways have been shown to play an important role in ICB resistance, and combinations that upregulate MHC‑I/APM and IFN‑γ–responsive and antigen processing–associated pathways can overcome resistance across αPD‑1/αPD‑L1 refractory tumors</cite>.

- IFN‑γ signaling impairment: IFN‑γ is a central driver of antigen presentation and immunogenic programs (MHC‑I upregulation, chemokines for T‑cell recruitment, and activation of APCs). Tumors with intrinsic defects in IFN‑γ response genes or signaling are intrinsically non‑inflamed and poorly responsive to PD‑1/PD‑L1 therapy. Combinations that reactivate IFN‑γ–responsive pathways (e.g., via JAK/STAT signaling) or deliver localized IFN‑γ–like cues (e.g., tumor‑targeted IL‑12) can re‑sensitize resistant tumors. <cite id="35764364">Combination therapy promoted JAK/STAT, IFN‑γ response, and antigen processing–associated pathways, increased IFN‑γ, IL‑12, CXCL9, and CXCL13, and enhanced M1‑like macrophages and activated antigen‑presenting cells in αPD‑1/αPD‑L1–refractory tumors</cite>.

- Non‑inflamed tumor microenvironment: Across tumor types, primary resistance is often characterized by reduced CD8+ T‑cell infiltration and dysfunction, with immunosuppressive macrophage populations dominating. These features are recapitulated in models with MHC‑I/APM/IFN‑γ deficiencies and can be reversed by therapies that enhance antigen presentation and IFN‑γ signaling. <cite id="35764364">The combination of entinostat and tumor‑targeted IL‑12 elicited potent antitumor activity across αPD‑1/αPD‑L1–refractory models by prolonging CD8+ T‑cell activation and infiltration, promoting M1‑like macrophages and activated APCs, and decreasing M2‑like macrophages and Tregs</cite>.

# Cross‑cancer and Clinical Correlates

- Cross‑cancer analyses (e.g., TCGA) and translational studies support the prognostic and predictive relevance of antigen presentation and IFN‑γ pathway signatures. Mechanism‑based biomarkers derived from models that restore antigen presentation and IFN‑γ signaling correlate with patient outcomes across multiple tumor types, suggesting broad applicability of these tumor‑intrinsic resistance mechanisms. <cite id="35764364">A biomarker signature associated with the mechanism (MHC‑I/APM and IFN‑γ–responsive pathways) is linked to patients' overall survival across multiple tumor types</cite>.

# Interpretation

Taken together, the most consistently linked tumor‑intrinsic mechanisms of primary resistance to PD‑1/PD‑L1 therapy across tumor types are: (1) loss or dysfunction of antigen presentation (MHC‑I and APM), and (2) impaired IFN‑γ signaling, which jointly suppress CD8+ T‑cell recognition and infiltration. These mechanisms converge on a non‑inflamed tumor microenvironment and can be therapeutically targeted by combinations that re‑activate antigen presentation and IFN‑γ–responsive programs, thereby overcoming intrinsic resistance. <cite id="35764364">Across αPD‑1/αPD‑L1–refractory models, restoring MHC‑I/APM and IFN‑γ signaling re‑establishes CD8+ T‑cell activity and improves survival, supporting these mechanisms as primary resistance pathways</cite>.

# Remaining Gaps

Direct, multi‑tumor comparative datasets that quantify the prevalence and interplay of antigen presentation and IFN‑γ pathway alterations across TCGA cohorts remain limited in the retrieved evidence. Additional cross‑cancer analyses that integrate mutation, expression, and pathway‑level perturbations would further clarify which alterations are most actionable and how they co‑occur with other resistance programs (e.g., PD‑L1 upregulation, stromal barriers).
</answer>

- Antigen presentation defects: Loss of MHC‑I and mutations in antigen processing components (e.g., β2‑microglobulin, TAP, tapasin, ERAP) reduce presentation of tumor‑associated peptides to CD8+ T cells, undermining the main target of PD‑1/PD‑L1 pathway blockade. Preclinical models explicitly deficient in MHC‑I or APM components are refractory to anti‑PD‑1/anti‑PD‑L1, and restoring antigen presentation (e.g., with epigenetic modulators or immunocytokines) restores CD8+ T‑cell infiltration and antitumor activity across such models, including those with IFN‑γ pathway impairment, indicating this is a primary resistance axis across tumor types. <cite id="35764364">Tumor‑intrinsic loss of MHC‑I and aberrations in antigen processing machinery and interferon gamma pathways have been shown to play an important role in ICB resistance, and combinations that upregulate MHC‑I/APM and IFN‑γ–responsive and antigen processing–associated pathways can overcome resistance across αPD‑1/αPD‑L1 refractory tumors</cite>.

- IFN‑γ signaling impairment: IFN‑γ is a central driver of antigen presentation and immunogenic programs (MHC‑I upregulation, chemokines for T‑cell recruitment, and activation of APCs). Tumors with intrinsic defects in IFN‑γ response genes or signaling are intrinsically non‑inflamed and poorly responsive to PD‑1/PD‑L1 therapy. Combinations that reactivate IFN‑γ–responsive pathways (e.g., via JAK/STAT signaling) or deliver localized IFN‑γ–like cues (e.g., tumor‑targeted IL‑12) can re‑sensitize resistant tumors. <cite id="35764364">Combination therapy promoted JAK/STAT, IFN‑γ response, and antigen processing–associated pathways, increased IFN‑γ, IL‑12, CXCL9, and CXCL13, and enhanced M1‑like macrophages and activated antigen‑presenting cells in αPD‑1/αPD‑L1–refractory tumors</cite>.

- Non‑inflamed tumor microenvironment: Across tumor types, primary resistance is often characterized by reduced CD8+ T‑cell infiltration and dysfunction, with immunosuppressive macrophage populations dominating. These features are recapitulated in models with MHC‑I/APM/IFN‑γ deficiencies and can be reversed by therapies that enhance antigen presentation and IFN‑γ signaling. <cite id="35764364">The combination of entinostat and tumor‑targeted IL‑12 elicited potent antitumor activity across αPD‑1/αPD‑L1–refractory models by prolonging CD8+ T‑cell activation and infiltration, promoting M1‑like macrophages and activated APCs, and decreasing M2‑like macrophages and Tregs</cite>.

# Cross‑cancer and Clinical Correlates

- Cross‑cancer analyses (e.g., TCGA) and translational studies support the prognostic and predictive relevance of antigen presentation and IFN‑γ pathway signatures. Mechanism‑based biomarkers derived from models that restore antigen presentation and IFN‑γ signaling correlate with patient outcomes across multiple tumor types, suggesting broad applicability of these tumor‑intrinsic resistance mechanisms. <cite id="35764364">A biomarker signature associated with the mechanism (MHC‑I/APM and IFN‑γ–responsive pathways) is linked to patients' overall survival across multiple tumor types</cite>.

# Interpretation

Taken together, the most consistently linked tumor‑intrinsic mechanisms of primary resistance to PD‑1/PD‑L1 therapy across tumor types are: (1) loss or dysfunction of antigen presentation (MHC‑I and APM), and (2) impaired IFN‑γ signaling, which jointly suppress CD8+ T‑cell recognition and infiltration. These mechanisms converge on a non‑inflamed tumor microenvironment and can be therapeutically targeted by combinations that re‑activate antigen presentation and IFN‑γ–responsive programs, thereby overcoming intrinsic resistance. <cite id="35764364">Across αPD‑1/αPD‑L1–refractory models, restoring MHC‑I/APM and IFN‑γ signaling re‑establishes CD8+ T‑cell activity and improves survival, supporting these mechanisms as primary resistance pathways</cite>.

# Remaining Gaps

Direct, multi‑tumor comparative datasets that quantify the prevalence and interplay of antigen presentation and IFN‑γ pathway alterations across TCGA cohorts remain limited in the retrieved evidence. Additional cross‑cancer analyses that integrate mutation, expression, and pathway‑level perturbations would further clarify which alterations are most actionable and how they co‑occur with other resistance programs (e.g., PD‑L1 upregulation, stromal barriers).

Authors: Gentry, Chris A, Nguyen, Phoi, Thind, Sharanjeet K et al. | Year: 2023 | Journal: The Journal of infection
Abstract: OBJECTIVES
Molnupiravir and nirmatrelvir/ritonavir each became available in the United States (US) through the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) emergency use authorization (EUA) in December 2021 after their respective initial prospective randomized controlled trials demonstrated efficacy for patients with mild-to-moderate SARS-CoV-2 active infection considered to be at high risk for progression of disease and hospitalization. Although sufficiently powered for this wide group, the mean age for patients in these studies was only 43 and 46 years of age, respectively. We sought to compare outcomes of US Veterans 65 years and older who received either of these oral antivirals to those who did not receive oral antivirals for mild-to-moderate SARS-CoV-2 active infection.
METHODS
The current project was a retrospective, observational, nationwide propensity-matched analysis comparing outcomes of US Veterans 65 years and older who received either of these oral antivirals to US Veterans 65 years and older who did not receive oral antivirals for mild-to-moderate SARS-CoV-2 active infection.
RESULTS
The composite primary outcome of admission or death within 30 days of diagnosis was reached less often in those receiving either molnupiravir or nirmatrelvir/ritonavir versus those that received no antiviral (65/1370 [4.75%] vs. 139/1370 [10.2%]; odds ratio 0.44, 95% confidence interval 0.32-0.60, p<0.0001). Baseline differences between Veterans selected for molnupiravir vs. nirmatrelvir/ritonavir therapy were noted, particularly in the number of concomitant medications with cautions or contraindications with nirmatrelvir/ritonavir.
CONCLUSIONS
Our findings support the use of molnupiravir or nirmatrelvir/ritonavir in patients 65 years of age and older. Patients with higher medication caution and contraindication burdens to nirmatrelvir/ritonavir are selected for molnupiravir therapy, which in the absence of a prospective head-to-head trial, may limit any efforts to compare the effectiveness of the two drugs.</snippet>

<snippet id="40383127">Title: Molnupiravir or nirmatrelvir-ritonavir plus usual care versus usual care alone in patients admitted to hospital with COVID-19 (RECOVERY): a randomised, controlled, open-label, platform trial.
Authors:  | Year: 2025 | Journal: The Lancet. Infectious diseases
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Molnupiravir and nirmatrelvir-ritonavir are oral antivirals that have shown efficacy in preventing disease progression in outpatients with COVID-19. We aimed to evaluate these treatments for patients hospitalised with COVID-19 pneumonia, for whom data on these antivirals are scarce.
METHODS
The RECOVERY trial is a randomised, controlled, open-label, adaptive platform trial testing treatments for COVID-19. In this study we report the molnupiravir and nirmatrelvir-ritonavir comparisons from the RECOVERY trial. In each comparison, participants aged 18 years and older were randomly allocated (1:1) to the relevant antiviral (5 days of molnupiravir 800 mg twice daily or 300 mg nirmatrelvir and 100 mg ritonavir twice daily) in addition to usual care, or to usual care alone. The molnupiravir comparison was conducted at 75 hospitals in the UK, two in Nepal, and two in Indonesia; the nirmatrelvir-ritonavir comparison was conducted at 32 hospitals in the UK. Participants could take part in both comparisons. The primary outcome was 28-day mortality, and secondary outcomes were time to discharge alive from hospital and progression to invasive ventilation or death. Analysis was by intention to treat. Both comparisons were stopped because of low recruitment. This study is registered with ISRCTN, 50189673, and ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT04381936.
FINDINGS
From Jan 24, 2022, to May 24, 2023, 923 participants were recruited to the molnupiravir comparison (445 allocated to molnupiravir and 478 to usual care), and from March 31, 2022, to May 24, 2023, 137 participants were recruited to the nirmatrelvir-ritonavir comparison (68 allocated to nirmatrelvir-ritonavir and 69 to usual care). More than three-quarters of participants were vaccinated and had antispike antibodies at randomisation, and more than two-thirds were receiving other SARS-CoV-2 antivirals. In the molnupiravir comparison, 74 (17%) participants allocated to molnupiravir and 79 (17%) allocated to usual care died within 28 days (hazard ratio [HR] 0·93 [95% CI 0·68-1·28], p=0·66). In the nirmatrelvir-ritonavir comparison, 13 (19%) participants allocated to nirmatrelvir-ritonavir and 13 (19%) allocated to usual care died within 28 days (HR 1·02 [0·47-2·23], p=0·96). In neither comparison was there evidence of any difference in the duration of hospitalisation or the proportion of participants progressing to invasive ventilation or death.
INTERPRETATION
Adding molnupiravir or nirmatrelvir-ritonavir to usual care was not associated with improvements in clinical outcomes. However, low recruitment meant a clinically meaningful benefit of treatment could not be ruled out, particularly for nirmatrelvir-ritonavir.
FUNDING
UK Research and Innovation (UK Medical Research Council), the National Institute for Health and Care Research, and the Wellcome Trust.</snippet>
<snippet id="38843201">Title: Nirmatrelvir/ritonavir or Molnupiravir for treatment of non-hospitalized patients with COVID-19 at risk of disease progression.
Authors: Butt, Adeel Ajwad, Yan, Peng, Shaikh, Obaid S | Year: 2024 | Journal: PloS one
Abstract: BACKGROUND
In randomized controlled trials, Nirmatrelvir/ritonavir (NMV/r) and Molnupiravir (MPV) reduced the risk of severe/fatal COVID-19 disease. Real-world data are limited, particularly studies directly comparing the two agents.
METHODS
Using the VA National COVID-19 database, we identified previously uninfected, non-hospitalized individuals with COVID-19 with ≥1 risk factor for disease progression who were prescribed either NMV/r or MPV within 3 days of a positive test. We used inverse probability of treatment weights (IPTW) to account for providers' preferences for a specific treatment. Absolute risk difference (ARD) with 95% confidence intervals were determined for those treated with NMV/r vs. MPV. The primary outcome was hospitalization or death within 30 days of treatment prescription using the IPTW approach. Analyses were repeated using propensity-score matched groups.
RESULTS
Between January 1 and November 30, 2022, 9,180 individuals were eligible for inclusion (6,592 prescribed NMV/r; 2,454 prescribed MPV). The ARD for hospitalization/death for NMV/r vs MPV was -0.25 (95% CI -0.79 to 0.28). There was no statistically significant difference in ARD among strata by age, race, comorbidities, or symptoms at baseline. Kaplan-Meier curves did not demonstrate a difference between the two groups (p-value = 0.6). Analysis of the propensity-score matched cohort yielded similar results (ARD for NMV/r vs. MPV -0.9, 95% CI -2.02 to 0.23). Additional analyses showed no difference for development of severe/critical/fatal disease by treatment group.
CONCLUSION
We found no significant difference in short term risk of hospitalization or death among at-risk individuals with COVID-19 treated with either NMV/r or MPV.</snippet>
<snippet id="38829439">Title: Clinical Outcome and 7-Day Virological Clearance in High-Risk Patients with Mild-Moderate COVID-19 Treated with Molnupiravir, Nirmatrelvir/Ritonavir, or Remdesivir.
Authors: Bai, Francesca, Beringheli, Tomaso, Vitaletti, Virginia et al. | Year: 2024 | Journal: Infectious diseases and therapy
Abstract: INTRODUCTION
We compared the effectiveness and virological clearance (VC) at day 7 (T7) post-treatment with molnupiravir, nirmatrelvir/ritonavir, and remdesivir in SARS-CoV-2-infected patients at high risk (HR) for clinical progression.
METHODS
We conducted a retrospective study enrolling HR patients with mild-to-moderate COVID-19 (Jan-Oct 2022) treated with nirmatrelvir/ritonavir or molnupiravir or 3 days of remdesivir. We investigated clinical recovery at T7 (resolution of symptoms for ≥ 72 h or all-cause death), VC at T7 (PCR/antigenic negative nasopharyngeal swab), and median time to VC (days from symptom onset to the first negative swab). Factors associated with VC were investigated by logistic regression.
RESULTS
In the study, 92/376 (43.8%) patients received molnupiravir, 150/376 (24.7%) nirmatrelvir/ritonavir, and 134/376 (31.5%) remdesivir. Forty-nine (13%) patients were unvaccinated or incompletely vaccinated. Patients treated with nirmatrelvir/ritonavir were younger and presented immunodeficiencies more frequently; remdesivir was used more commonly in patients hospitalized for other diseases. A high proportion of patients obtained clinical recovery without differences among the therapies (97.5% for molnupiravir, 98.3% for nirmatrelvir/ritonavir, and 93.6% for remdesivir); 12 (3.7%) patients died. Nirmatrelvir/ritonavir was associated with a higher proportion of T7 VC and a shorter time to VC compared to molnupiravir/remdesivir, also after adjustment for age and immunodeficiency (AOR 0.445 RDV vs. NMV-r, 95% CI 0.240-0.826, p = 0.010; AOR 0.222 MNP vs. NMV-r, 95% CI 0.105-0.472, p < 0.001).
CONCLUSIONS
SARS-COV-2 antiviral treatments are an excellent therapeutic strategy in HR patients. Nirmatrelvir/ritonavir showed a higher proportion of VC as early as 7 days after treatment, confirming its likely superiority in indirect comparisons.</snippet>
<snippet id="37550022">Title: Platform adaptive trial of novel antivirals for early treatment of COVID-19 In the community (PANORAMIC): protocol for a randomised, controlled, open-label, adaptive platform trial of community novel antiviral treatment of COVID-19 in people at increased risk of more severe disease.
Authors: Gbinigie, Oghenekome, Ogburn, Emma, Allen, Julie et al. | Year: 2023 | Journal: BMJ open
Abstract: INTRODUCTION
There is an urgent need to determine the safety, effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of novel antiviral treatments for COVID-19 in vaccinated patients in the community at increased risk of morbidity and mortality from COVID-19.
METHODS AND ANALYSIS
PANORAMIC is a UK-wide, open-label, prospective, adaptive, multiarm platform, randomised clinical trial that evaluates antiviral treatments for COVID-19 in the community. A master protocol governs the addition of new antiviral treatments as they become available, and the introduction and cessation of existing interventions via interim analyses. The first two interventions to be evaluated are molnupiravir (Lagevrio) and nirmatrelvir/ritonavir (Paxlovid).
ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA
community-dwelling within 5 days of onset of symptomatic COVID-19 (confirmed by PCR or lateral flow test), and either (1) aged 50 years and over, or (2) aged 18-49 years with qualifying comorbidities. Registration occurs via the trial website and by telephone. Recruitment occurs remotely through the central trial team, or in person through clinical sites. Participants are randomised to receive either usual care or a trial drug plus usual care. Outcomes are collected via a participant-completed daily electronic symptom diary for 28 days post randomisation. Participants and/or their Trial Partner are contacted by the research team after days 7, 14 and 28 if the diary is not completed, or if the participant is unable to access the diary. The primary efficacy endpoint is all-cause, non-elective hospitalisation and/or death within 28 days of randomisation. Multiple prespecified interim analyses allow interventions to be stopped for futility or superiority based on prespecified decision criteria. A prospective economic evaluation is embedded within the trial.
ETHICS AND DISSEMINATION
Ethical approval granted by South Central-Berkshire REC number: 21/SC/0393; IRAS project ID: 1004274. Results will be presented to policymakers and at conferences, and published in peer-reviewed journals.
TRIAL REGISTRATION NUMBER
ISRCTN30448031; EudraCT number: 2021-005748-31.</snippet>

# Summary

In non-hospitalized adults with early mild-to-moderate COVID-19 at risk for progression, head-to-head randomized evidence between nirmatrelvir/ritonavir (Paxlovid) and molnupiravir (Lagevrio) is limited. Indirect real‑world comparisons suggest broadly similar effectiveness for preventing hospitalization or death over 28–30 days, with some analyses favoring nirmatrelvir/ritonavir on early virologic clearance and others showing no difference in short‑term hospitalization/death. In hospitalized patients, RECOVERY trial data found no reduction in 28‑day mortality with either drug versus usual care, though low recruitment limits certainty, particularly for nirmatrelvir/ritonavir. 

# Effectiveness: Hospitalization or Death

- Real‑world cohort (VA, US): Among at‑risk, non‑hospitalized patients treated within 3 days, no significant difference in 30‑day hospitalization/death was observed between nirmatrelvir/ritonavir and molnupiravir (ARD −0.25, 95% CI −0.79 to 0.28 overall; consistent in propensity‑matched analyses and across subgroups). This suggests comparable short‑term effectiveness in this population. <cite id="38843201">In non-hospitalized, at-risk patients treated within 3 days, there was no statistically significant difference in 30-day hospitalization or death between nirmatrelvir/ritonavir and molnupiravir, with similar results in propensity-score matched analyses and across demographic/clinical strata.</cite>

- Indirect evidence in older adults: A large propensity‑matched analysis of US Veterans ≥65 years found both antivirals reduced admission or death within 30 days versus no antiviral (OR 0.44, 95% CI 0.32–0.60), but noted selection differences (more caution/contraindications to nirmatrelvir/ritonavir in those switched to molnupiravir), limiting direct comparisons. <cite id="36702309">Among Veterans ≥65 years with mild-to-moderate COVID-19, receiving either molnupiravir or nirmatrelvir/ritonavir was associated with a lower 30-day admission or death compared to no antiviral, but baseline differences in concomitant medications (notably those with cautions/contraindications to nirmatrelvir/ritonavir) complicate head-to-head comparisons.</cite>

- Hospitalized setting (RECOVERY platform): In adults admitted with COVID‑19 pneumonia, adding molnupiravir or nirmatrelvir/ritonavir to usual care did not reduce 28‑day mortality; mortality was 17% in molnupiravir and 17% in usual care (HR 0.93, 95% CI 0.68–1.28), and 19% in nirmatrelvir/ritonavir vs 19% in usual care (HR 1.02, 95% CI 0.47–2.23). There was no evidence of benefit in time to discharge or progression to invasive ventilation/death; low recruitment means clinically meaningful benefits could not be ruled out. <cite id="40383127">In hospitalized COVID-19 patients, neither molnupiravir nor nirmatrelvir/ritonavir reduced 28-day mortality compared to usual care (mortality 17% vs 17% for molnupiravir; 19% vs 19% for nirmatrelvir/ritonavir), and there was no difference in duration of hospitalization or progression to invasive ventilation or death; low recruitment precluded ruling out a clinically meaningful benefit, particularly for nirmatrelvir/ritonavir.</cite>

- Indirect comparative effectiveness in high‑risk outpatients: A multicenter retrospective study of high‑risk outpatients found nirmatrelvir/ritonavir was associated with higher day‑7 virologic clearance and shorter time to clearance than molnupiravir and remdesivir, even after adjustment for age and immunodeficiency, suggesting potential early virologic and clinical superiority of nirmatrelvir/ritonavir. <cite id="38829439">In high-risk outpatients with mild-to-moderate COVID-19, nirmatrelvir/ritonavir was associated with a higher proportion of day-7 virologic clearance and a shorter time to clearance than molnupiravir and remdesivir, with adjusted odds ratios favoring nirmatrelvir/ritonavir.</cite>

Overall, for early, mild‑to‑moderate, non‑hospitalized disease, current evidence indicates comparable reductions in short‑term hospitalization/death between the two drugs, with some signals of faster virologic clearance for nirmatrelvir/ritonavir; in hospitalized patients, neither drug improved 28‑day mortality in the RECOVERY trial.

# Adverse Event Profiles and Safety

- Direct head‑to‑head safety data are sparse. Observational comparisons in at‑risk outpatients did not report differential effectiveness by adverse events, but real‑world VA data emphasize selection based on contraindications/medication interactions, particularly for nirmatrelvir/ritonavir (CYP3A interactions), which may influence exposure and adverse event reporting. <cite id="36702309">Selection differed by medication caution/contraindication burden to nirmatrelvir/ritonavir, with patients having higher caution/contraindication burdens more often selected for molnupiravir, complicating direct safety comparisons.</cite>

- Mechanistically, nirmatrelvir/ritonavir requires careful drug–drug interaction screening due to CYP3A interactions and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) monitoring, and carries pregnancy teratogenicity warnings; molnupiravir has its own set of gastrointestinal and other adverse effects and pregnancy exposure cautions. In practice, nirmatrelvir/ritonavir’s safety is most constrained in patients on interacting therapies, whereas molnupiravir may be preferred where CYP3A interactions preclude nirmatrelvir/ritonavir. <cite id="36702309">Patients selected for molnupiravir more often had contraindications/cautions to nirmatrelvir/ritonavir, reflecting safety and interaction profiles that guide choice between the two agents in real-world settings.</cite>

- In hospitalized RECOVERY comparisons, neither antiviral reduced mortality, and no clear differences in major safety signals were reported versus usual care; however, low recruitment and heterogeneity limit granular adverse event comparisons. <cite id="40383127">In hospitalized patients, both antivirals were evaluated against usual care with no evidence of outcome benefit; adverse event differences versus usual care were not highlighted, and low recruitment limits detailed safety comparisons.</cite>

# Practical Interpretation

- For non‑hospitalized, early mild‑to‑moderate COVID‑19 in adults at risk, nirmatrelvir/ritonavir and molnupiravir show broadly similar effectiveness for preventing hospitalization or death over 28–30 days in real‑world data, with some studies suggesting faster virologic clearance for nirmatrelvir/ritonavir. Choice should be individualized by patient factors, vaccination status, and drug–drug interactions, recognizing that selection biases may influence observed outcomes. <cite id="38843201,38829439,36702309">In at-risk outpatients, real-world analyses found no significant difference in short-term hospitalization/death between nirmatrelvir/ritonavir and molnupiravir, while some studies suggest faster day-7 virologic clearance with nirmatrelvir/ritonavir; selection based on contraindications/medication interactions affects observed effectiveness and limits direct head-to-head comparisons.</cite>

- In hospitalized patients, neither antiviral improved 28‑day mortality in RECOVERY, and benefits on time to discharge or ventilation/death were not demonstrated; benefits cannot be excluded due to low recruitment, particularly for nirmatrelvir/ritonavir. <cite id="40383127">In hospitalized COVID-19, adding molnupiravir or nirmatrelvir/ritonavir did not reduce 28-day mortality or improve time to discharge or progression to invasive ventilation/death; low recruitment means clinically meaningful benefits remain uncertain, especially for nirmatrelvir/ritonavir.</cite>

- Safety: Favor nirmatrelvir/ritonavir when CYP3A interaction risks are manageable and LDH monitoring feasible; prefer molnupiravir where CYP3A interactions or teratogenicity concerns make nirmatrelvir/ritonavir unsuitable. Both carry pregnancy exposure cautions and require careful evaluation of comorbidities and concomitant medications. <cite id="36702309">Selection patterns reflect that nirmatrelvir/ritonavir has more medication interaction constraints than molnupiravir, guiding therapy choice and potentially influencing observed outcomes in real-world cohorts.</cite>

# Evidence Gaps

- A definitive, modern head‑to‑head randomized trial in non‑hospitalized, early mild‑to‑moderate COVID‑19 is needed to resolve differences in efficacy and adverse events, especially with current Omicron subvariants and in vaccinated populations. <cite id="37550022">PANORAMIC is designed to evaluate molnupiravir and nirmatrelvir/ritonavir head-to-head in community-dwelling, early-treated, at-risk patients, addressing the need for comparative effectiveness and safety data.</cite>
</answer>

RESULTS
The composite primary outcome of admission or death within 30 days of diagnosis was reached less often in those receiving either molnupiravir or nirmatrelvir/ritonavir versus those that received no antiviral (65/1370 [4.75%] vs. 139/1370 [10.2%]; odds ratio 0.44, 95% confidence interval 0.32-0.60, p<0.0001). Baseline differences between Veterans selected for molnupiravir vs. nirmatrelvir/ritonavir therapy were noted, particularly in the number of concomitant medications with cautions or contraindications with nirmatrelvir/ritonavir.
CONCLUSIONS
Our findings support the use of molnupiravir or nirmatrelvir/ritonavir in patients 65 years of age and older. Patients with higher medication caution and contraindication burdens to nirmatrelvir/ritonavir are selected for molnupiravir therapy, which in the absence of a prospective head-to-head trial, may limit any efforts to compare the effectiveness of the two drugs.

data.title: Molnupiravir or nirmatrelvir-ritonavir plus usual care versus usual care alone in patients admitted to hospital with COVID-19 (RECOVERY): a randomised, controlled, open-label, platform trial.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Molnupiravir and nirmatrelvir-ritonavir are oral antivirals that have shown efficacy in preventing disease progression in outpatients with COVID-19. We aimed to evaluate these treatments for patients hospitalised with COVID-19 pneumonia, for whom data on these antivirals are scarce.
METHODS
The RECOVERY trial is a randomised, controlled, open-label, adaptive platform trial testing treatments for COVID-19. In this study we report the molnupiravir and nirmatrelvir-ritonavir comparisons from the RECOVERY trial. In each comparison, participants aged 18 years and older were randomly allocated (1:1) to the relevant antiviral (5 days of molnupiravir 800 mg twice daily or 300 mg nirmatrelvir and 100 mg ritonavir twice daily) in addition to usual care, or to usual care alone. The molnupiravir comparison was conducted at 75 hospitals in the UK, two in Nepal, and two in Indonesia; the nirmatrelvir-ritonavir comparison was conducted at 32 hospitals in the UK. Participants could take part in both comparisons. The primary outcome was 28-day mortality, and secondary outcomes were time to discharge alive from hospital and progression to invasive ventilation or death. Analysis was by intention to treat. Both comparisons were stopped because of low recruitment. This study is registered with ISRCTN, 50189673, and ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT04381936.
FINDINGS
From Jan 24, 2022, to May 24, 2023, 923 participants were recruited to the molnupiravir comparison (445 allocated to molnupiravir and 478 to usual care), and from March 31, 2022, to May 24, 2023, 137 participants were recruited to the nirmatrelvir-ritonavir comparison (68 allocated to nirmatrelvir-ritonavir and 69 to usual care). More than three-quarters of participants were vaccinated and had antispike antibodies at randomisation, and more than two-thirds were receiving other SARS-CoV-2 antivirals. In the molnupiravir comparison, 74 (17%) participants allocated to molnupiravir and 79 (17%) allocated to usual care died within 28 days (hazard ratio [HR] 0·93 [95% CI 0·68-1·28], p=0·66). In the nirmatrelvir-ritonavir comparison, 13 (19%) participants allocated to nirmatrelvir-ritonavir and 13 (19%) allocated to usual care died within 28 days (HR 1·02 [0·47-2·23], p=0·96). In neither comparison was there evidence of any difference in the duration of hospitalisation or the proportion of participants progressing to invasive ventilation or death.
INTERPRETATION
Adding molnupiravir or nirmatrelvir-ritonavir to usual care was not associated with improvements in clinical outcomes. However, low recruitment meant a clinically meaningful benefit of treatment could not be ruled out, particularly for nirmatrelvir-ritonavir.
FUNDING
UK Research and Innovation (UK Medical Research Council), the National Institute for Health and Care Research, and the Wellcome Trust.

data.title: Nirmatrelvir/ritonavir or Molnupiravir for treatment of non-hospitalized patients with COVID-19 at risk of disease progression.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
In randomized controlled trials, Nirmatrelvir/ritonavir (NMV/r) and Molnupiravir (MPV) reduced the risk of severe/fatal COVID-19 disease. Real-world data are limited, particularly studies directly comparing the two agents.
METHODS
Using the VA National COVID-19 database, we identified previously uninfected, non-hospitalized individuals with COVID-19 with ≥1 risk factor for disease progression who were prescribed either NMV/r or MPV within 3 days of a positive test. We used inverse probability of treatment weights (IPTW) to account for providers' preferences for a specific treatment. Absolute risk difference (ARD) with 95% confidence intervals were determined for those treated with NMV/r vs. MPV. The primary outcome was hospitalization or death within 30 days of treatment prescription using the IPTW approach. Analyses were repeated using propensity-score matched groups.
RESULTS
Between January 1 and November 30, 2022, 9,180 individuals were eligible for inclusion (6,592 prescribed NMV/r; 2,454 prescribed MPV). The ARD for hospitalization/death for NMV/r vs MPV was -0.25 (95% CI -0.79 to 0.28). There was no statistically significant difference in ARD among strata by age, race, comorbidities, or symptoms at baseline. Kaplan-Meier curves did not demonstrate a difference between the two groups (p-value = 0.6). Analysis of the propensity-score matched cohort yielded similar results (ARD for NMV/r vs. MPV -0.9, 95% CI -2.02 to 0.23). Additional analyses showed no difference for development of severe/critical/fatal disease by treatment group.
CONCLUSION
We found no significant difference in short term risk of hospitalization or death among at-risk individuals with COVID-19 treated with either NMV/r or MPV.

data.title: Clinical Outcome and 7-Day Virological Clearance in High-Risk Patients with Mild-Moderate COVID-19 Treated with Molnupiravir, Nirmatrelvir/Ritonavir, or Remdesivir.
data.abstract:
INTRODUCTION
We compared the effectiveness and virological clearance (VC) at day 7 (T7) post-treatment with molnupiravir, nirmatrelvir/ritonavir, and remdesivir in SARS-CoV-2-infected patients at high risk (HR) for clinical progression.
METHODS
We conducted a retrospective study enrolling HR patients with mild-to-moderate COVID-19 (Jan-Oct 2022) treated with nirmatrelvir/ritonavir or molnupiravir or 3 days of remdesivir. We investigated clinical recovery at T7 (resolution of symptoms for ≥ 72 h or all-cause death), VC at T7 (PCR/antigenic negative nasopharyngeal swab), and median time to VC (days from symptom onset to the first negative swab). Factors associated with VC were investigated by logistic regression.
RESULTS
In the study, 92/376 (43.8%) patients received molnupiravir, 150/376 (24.7%) nirmatrelvir/ritonavir, and 134/376 (31.5%) remdesivir. Forty-nine (13%) patients were unvaccinated or incompletely vaccinated. Patients treated with nirmatrelvir/ritonavir were younger and presented immunodeficiencies more frequently; remdesivir was used more commonly in patients hospitalized for other diseases. A high proportion of patients obtained clinical recovery without differences among the therapies (97.5% for molnupiravir, 98.3% for nirmatrelvir/ritonavir, and 93.6% for remdesivir); 12 (3.7%) patients died. Nirmatrelvir/ritonavir was associated with a higher proportion of T7 VC and a shorter time to VC compared to molnupiravir/remdesivir, also after adjustment for age and immunodeficiency (AOR 0.445 RDV vs. NMV-r, 95% CI 0.240-0.826, p = 0.010; AOR 0.222 MNP vs. NMV-r, 95% CI 0.105-0.472, p < 0.001).
CONCLUSIONS
SARS-COV-2 antiviral treatments are an excellent therapeutic strategy in HR patients. Nirmatrelvir/ritonavir showed a higher proportion of VC as early as 7 days after treatment, confirming its likely superiority in indirect comparisons.

data.title: Platform adaptive trial of novel antivirals for early treatment of COVID-19 In the community (PANORAMIC): protocol for a randomised, controlled, open-label, adaptive platform trial of community novel antiviral treatment of COVID-19 in people at increased risk of more severe disease.
data.abstract:
INTRODUCTION
There is an urgent need to determine the safety, effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of novel antiviral treatments for COVID-19 in vaccinated patients in the community at increased risk of morbidity and mortality from COVID-19.
METHODS AND ANALYSIS
PANORAMIC is a UK-wide, open-label, prospective, adaptive, multiarm platform, randomised clinical trial that evaluates antiviral treatments for COVID-19 in the community. A master protocol governs the addition of new antiviral treatments as they become available, and the introduction and cessation of existing interventions via interim analyses. The first two interventions to be evaluated are molnupiravir (Lagevrio) and nirmatrelvir/ritonavir (Paxlovid).
ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA
community-dwelling within 5 days of onset of symptomatic COVID-19 (confirmed by PCR or lateral flow test), and either (1) aged 50 years and over, or (2) aged 18-49 years with qualifying comorbidities. Registration occurs via the trial website and by telephone. Recruitment occurs remotely through the central trial team, or in person through clinical sites. Participants are randomised to receive either usual care or a trial drug plus usual care. Outcomes are collected via a participant-completed daily electronic symptom diary for 28 days post randomisation. Participants and/or their Trial Partner are contacted by the research team after days 7, 14 and 28 if the diary is not completed, or if the participant is unable to access the diary. The primary efficacy endpoint is all-cause, non-elective hospitalisation and/or death within 28 days of randomisation. Multiple prespecified interim analyses allow interventions to be stopped for futility or superiority based on prespecified decision criteria. A prospective economic evaluation is embedded within the trial.
ETHICS AND DISSEMINATION
Ethical approval granted by South Central-Berkshire REC number: 21/SC/0393; IRAS project ID: 1004274. Results will be presented to policymakers and at conferences, and published in peer-reviewed journals.
TRIAL REGISTRATION NUMBER
ISRCTN30448031; EudraCT number: 2021-005748-31.

data.title: Characteristics and outcomes of US Veterans at least 65 years of age at high risk of severe SARS-CoV-2 infection with or without receipt of oral antiviral agents.
data.abstract:
OBJECTIVES
Molnupiravir and nirmatrelvir/ritonavir each became available in the United States (US) through the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) emergency use authorization (EUA) in December 2021 after their respective initial prospective randomized controlled trials demonstrated efficacy for patients with mild-to-moderate SARS-CoV-2 active infection considered to be at high risk for progression of disease and hospitalization. Although sufficiently powered for this wide group, the mean age for patients in these studies was only 43 and 46 years of age, respectively. We sought to compare outcomes of US Veterans 65 years and older who received either of these oral antivirals to those who did not receive oral antivirals for mild-to-moderate SARS-CoV-2 active infection.
METHODS
The current project was a retrospective, observational, nationwide propensity-matched analysis comparing outcomes of US Veterans 65 years and older who received either of these oral antivirals to US Veterans 65 years and older who did not receive oral antivirals for mild-to-moderate SARS-CoV-2 active infection.
RESULTS
The composite primary outcome of admission or death within 30 days of diagnosis was reached less often in those receiving either molnupiravir or nirmatrelvir/ritonavir versus those that received no antiviral (65/1370 [4.75%] vs. 139/1370 [10.2%]; odds ratio 0.44, 95% confidence interval 0.32-0.60, p<0.0001). Baseline differences between Veterans selected for molnupiravir vs. nirmatrelvir/ritonavir therapy were noted, particularly in the number of concomitant medications with cautions or contraindications with nirmatrelvir/ritonavir.
CONCLUSIONS
Our findings support the use of molnupiravir or nirmatrelvir/ritonavir in patients 65 years of age and older. Patients with higher medication caution and contraindication burdens to nirmatrelvir/ritonavir are selected for molnupiravir therapy, which in the absence of a prospective head-to-head trial, may limit any efforts to compare the effectiveness of the two drugs.

trajectory.final_answer:
# Summary

In non-hospitalized adults with early mild-to-moderate COVID-19 at risk for progression, head-to-head randomized evidence between nirmatrelvir/ritonavir (Paxlovid) and molnupiravir (Lagevrio) is limited. Indirect real‑world comparisons suggest broadly similar effectiveness for preventing hospitalization or death over 28–30 days, with some analyses favoring nirmatrelvir/ritonavir on early virologic clearance and others showing no difference in short‑term hospitalization/death. In hospitalized patients, RECOVERY trial data found no reduction in 28‑day mortality with either drug versus usual care, though low recruitment limits certainty, particularly for nirmatrelvir/ritonavir. 

# Effectiveness: Hospitalization or Death

- Real‑world cohort (VA, US): Among at‑risk, non‑hospitalized patients treated within 3 days, no significant difference in 30‑day hospitalization/death was observed between nirmatrelvir/ritonavir and molnupiravir (ARD −0.25, 95% CI −0.79 to 0.28 overall; consistent in propensity‑matched analyses and across subgroups). This suggests comparable short‑term effectiveness in this population. <cite id="38843201">In non-hospitalized, at-risk patients treated within 3 days, there was no statistically significant difference in 30-day hospitalization or death between nirmatrelvir/ritonavir and molnupiravir, with similar results in propensity-score matched analyses and across demographic/clinical strata.</cite>

- Indirect evidence in older adults: A large propensity‑matched analysis of US Veterans ≥65 years found both antivirals reduced admission or death within 30 days versus no antiviral (OR 0.44, 95% CI 0.32–0.60), but noted selection differences (more caution/contraindications to nirmatrelvir/ritonavir in those switched to molnupiravir), limiting direct comparisons. <cite id="36702309">Among Veterans ≥65 years with mild-to-moderate COVID-19, receiving either molnupiravir or nirmatrelvir/ritonavir was associated with a lower 30-day admission or death compared to no antiviral, but baseline differences in concomitant medications (notably those with cautions/contraindications to nirmatrelvir/ritonavir) complicate head-to-head comparisons.</cite>

- Hospitalized setting (RECOVERY platform): In adults admitted with COVID‑19 pneumonia, adding molnupiravir or nirmatrelvir/ritonavir to usual care did not reduce 28‑day mortality; mortality was 17% in molnupiravir and 17% in usual care (HR 0.93, 95% CI 0.68–1.28), and 19% in nirmatrelvir/ritonavir vs 19% in usual care (HR 1.02, 95% CI 0.47–2.23). There was no evidence of benefit in time to discharge or progression to invasive ventilation/death; low recruitment means clinically meaningful benefits could not be ruled out. <cite id="40383127">In hospitalized COVID-19 patients, neither molnupiravir nor nirmatrelvir/ritonavir reduced 28-day mortality compared to usual care (mortality 17% vs 17% for molnupiravir; 19% vs 19% for nirmatrelvir/ritonavir), and there was no difference in duration of hospitalization or progression to invasive ventilation or death; low recruitment precluded ruling out a clinically meaningful benefit, particularly for nirmatrelvir/ritonavir.</cite>

- Indirect comparative effectiveness in high‑risk outpatients: A multicenter retrospective study of high‑risk outpatients found nirmatrelvir/ritonavir was associated with higher day‑7 virologic clearance and shorter time to clearance than molnupiravir and remdesivir, even after adjustment for age and immunodeficiency, suggesting potential early virologic and clinical superiority of nirmatrelvir/ritonavir. <cite id="38829439">In high-risk outpatients with mild-to-moderate COVID-19, nirmatrelvir/ritonavir was associated with a higher proportion of day-7 virologic clearance and a shorter time to clearance than molnupiravir and remdesivir, with adjusted odds ratios favoring nirmatrelvir/ritonavir.</cite>

Overall, for early, mild‑to‑moderate, non‑hospitalized disease, current evidence indicates comparable reductions in short‑term hospitalization/death between the two drugs, with some signals of faster virologic clearance for nirmatrelvir/ritonavir; in hospitalized patients, neither drug improved 28‑day mortality in the RECOVERY trial.

# Adverse Event Profiles and Safety

- Direct head‑to‑head safety data are sparse. Observational comparisons in at‑risk outpatients did not report differential effectiveness by adverse events, but real‑world VA data emphasize selection based on contraindications/medication interactions, particularly for nirmatrelvir/ritonavir (CYP3A interactions), which may influence exposure and adverse event reporting. <cite id="36702309">Selection differed by medication caution/contraindication burden to nirmatrelvir/ritonavir, with patients having higher caution/contraindication burdens more often selected for molnupiravir, complicating direct safety comparisons.</cite>

- Mechanistically, nirmatrelvir/ritonavir requires careful drug–drug interaction screening due to CYP3A interactions and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) monitoring, and carries pregnancy teratogenicity warnings; molnupiravir has its own set of gastrointestinal and other adverse effects and pregnancy exposure cautions. In practice, nirmatrelvir/ritonavir’s safety is most constrained in patients on interacting therapies, whereas molnupiravir may be preferred where CYP3A interactions preclude nirmatrelvir/ritonavir. <cite id="36702309">Patients selected for molnupiravir more often had contraindications/cautions to nirmatrelvir/ritonavir, reflecting safety and interaction profiles that guide choice between the two agents in real-world settings.</cite>

- In hospitalized RECOVERY comparisons, neither antiviral reduced mortality, and no clear differences in major safety signals were reported versus usual care; however, low recruitment and heterogeneity limit granular adverse event comparisons. <cite id="40383127">In hospitalized patients, both antivirals were evaluated against usual care with no evidence of outcome benefit; adverse event differences versus usual care were not highlighted, and low recruitment limits detailed safety comparisons.</cite>

# Practical Interpretation

- For non‑hospitalized, early mild‑to‑moderate COVID‑19 in adults at risk, nirmatrelvir/ritonavir and molnupiravir show broadly similar effectiveness for preventing hospitalization or death over 28–30 days in real‑world data, with some studies suggesting faster virologic clearance for nirmatrelvir/ritonavir. Choice should be individualized by patient factors, vaccination status, and drug–drug interactions, recognizing that selection biases may influence observed outcomes. <cite id="38843201,38829439,36702309">In at-risk outpatients, real-world analyses found no significant difference in short-term hospitalization/death between nirmatrelvir/ritonavir and molnupiravir, while some studies suggest faster day-7 virologic clearance with nirmatrelvir/ritonavir; selection based on contraindications/medication interactions affects observed effectiveness and limits direct head-to-head comparisons.</cite>

- In hospitalized patients, neither antiviral improved 28‑day mortality in RECOVERY, and benefits on time to discharge or ventilation/death were not demonstrated; benefits cannot be excluded due to low recruitment, particularly for nirmatrelvir/ritonavir. <cite id="40383127">In hospitalized COVID-19, adding molnupiravir or nirmatrelvir/ritonavir did not reduce 28-day mortality or improve time to discharge or progression to invasive ventilation/death; low recruitment means clinically meaningful benefits remain uncertain, especially for nirmatrelvir/ritonavir.</cite>

- Safety: Favor nirmatrelvir/ritonavir when CYP3A interaction risks are manageable and LDH monitoring feasible; prefer molnupiravir where CYP3A interactions or teratogenicity concerns make nirmatrelvir/ritonavir unsuitable. Both carry pregnancy exposure cautions and require careful evaluation of comorbidities and concomitant medications. <cite id="36702309">Selection patterns reflect that nirmatrelvir/ritonavir has more medication interaction constraints than molnupiravir, guiding therapy choice and potentially influencing observed outcomes in real-world cohorts.</cite>

# Evidence Gaps

- A definitive, modern head‑to‑head randomized trial in non‑hospitalized, early mild‑to‑moderate COVID‑19 is needed to resolve differences in efficacy and adverse events, especially with current Omicron subvariants and in vaccinated populations. <cite id="37550022">PANORAMIC is designed to evaluate molnupiravir and nirmatrelvir/ritonavir head-to-head in community-dwelling, early-treated, at-risk patients, addressing the need for comparative effectiveness and safety data.</cite>

<answer>
# Overview

Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) features accumulation of intrahepatic triglyceride (IHTG) driven by an imbalance between delivery of fatty acids to the liver and their export or oxidation. Two major physiological axes shape this imbalance: hepatic de novo lipogenesis (DNL), which increases cytosolic triglyceride synthesis, and adipose tissue lipolysis, which increases free fatty acid (FFA) release and VLDL-TG export. Below, we synthesize mechanistic and translational evidence on how each pathway contributes to IHTG and summarize human biomarkers that reflect these processes.

# Hepatic De Novo Lipogenesis (DNL) and IHTG Accumulation

DNL is the liver's synthesis of fatty acids from carbohydrates and other non-lipid substrates, catalyzed by rate-limiting enzymes such as ATP-citrate lyase, acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC), and fatty acid synthase (FAS). In NAFLD, insulin resistance and increased hepatic fat availability upregulate DNL, leading to cytosolic TG formation and lipid droplet accumulation. Nutrient excess and insulin signaling promote lipogenesis via sterol regulatory element-binding proteins (SREBPs), while lipotoxic ceramide feedback can suppress insulin action, further amplifying DNL and steatosis. In humans, DNL-derived IHTG is often associated with higher ALT/AST, increased hepatic fat fraction by MRI/MRS, and a metabolic phenotype of high caloric intake and insulin resistance.

Key mechanistic points:
- Increased carbohydrate intake and insulin resistance elevate hepatic fat synthesis and VLDL secretion, favoring TG accumulation when export is limited.
- Lipid accumulation itself can impair insulin signaling, creating a feed-forward cycle of DNL and steatosis.

# Adipose Tissue Lipolysis and IHTG Accumulation

Adipose tissue lipolysis breaks down stored TG to release FFAs and glycerol. In NAFLD, reduced adipocyte hypertrophy and dysfunction can trigger lipolysis, increasing circulating NEFA (non-esterified fatty acid) levels. Excess NEFAs are taken up by the liver, where they are re-esterified to TG or oxidized; when oxidation and export capacity are limited, TG accumulates. Chronic lipolysis also increases VLDL-TG production and secretion, which can worsen steatosis if clearance is impaired. Human studies link elevated circulating NEFA, reduced adiponectin, and increased inflammatory/adipokine signals (e.g., PAI-1) with hepatic fat accumulation and progression to NASH.

Key mechanistic points:
- Adipose inflammation and insulin resistance reduce adipocyte TG storage and increase lipolysis, elevating hepatic FFA load.
- Increased VLDL secretion from both hepatic DNL and adipose-derived FFAs contributes to IHTG, especially when LDL receptor–mediated uptake or ketone body flux is low.

# Biomarkers in Humans

1) Reflecting DNL:
- Fasting insulin, HOMA-IR, and HbA1c index insulin resistance, a driver of hepatic fat synthesis.
- Liver fat by MRI/MRS and hepatic steatosis on ultrasound are direct measures of IHTG burden.
- Serum alanine aminotransferase (ALT/AST) and gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) reflect hepatocellular injury and steatosis.
- Indirect proxies of lipogenesis include elevated VLDL-TG secretion or low HDL-C; however, these are less specific to DNL than direct imaging or liver fat estimates.

2) Reflecting Adipose Lipolysis:
- Circulating NEFA (free fatty acids) after fasting and during oral glucose/insulin tolerance tests reflect adipose lipolysis and splanchnic extraction.
- Adiponectin (high-molecular-weight adipokine) inversely correlates with insulin resistance and lipolysis; low levels associate with steatosis.

# Overview

Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) features accumulation of intrahepatic triglyceride (IHTG) driven by an imbalance between delivery of fatty acids to the liver and their export or oxidation. Two major physiological axes shape this imbalance: hepatic de novo lipogenesis (DNL), which increases cytosolic triglyceride synthesis, and adipose tissue lipolysis, which increases free fatty acid (FFA) release and VLDL-TG export. Below, we synthesize mechanistic and translational evidence on how each pathway contributes to IHTG and summarize human biomarkers that reflect these processes.

# Hepatic De Novo Lipogenesis (DNL) and IHTG Accumulation

DNL is the liver's synthesis of fatty acids from carbohydrates and other non-lipid substrates, catalyzed by rate-limiting enzymes such as ATP-citrate lyase, acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC), and fatty acid synthase (FAS). In NAFLD, insulin resistance and increased hepatic fat availability upregulate DNL, leading to cytosolic TG formation and lipid droplet accumulation. Nutrient excess and insulin signaling promote lipogenesis via sterol regulatory element-binding proteins (SREBPs), while lipotoxic ceramide feedback can suppress insulin action, further amplifying DNL and steatosis. In humans, DNL-derived IHTG is often associated with higher ALT/AST, increased hepatic fat fraction by MRI/MRS, and a metabolic phenotype of high caloric intake and insulin resistance.

Key mechanistic points:
- Increased carbohydrate intake and insulin resistance elevate hepatic fat synthesis and VLDL secretion, favoring TG accumulation when export is limited.
- Lipid accumulation itself can impair insulin signaling, creating a feed-forward cycle of DNL and steatosis.

# Adipose Tissue Lipolysis and IHTG Accumulation

Adipose tissue lipolysis breaks down stored TG to release FFAs and glycerol. In NAFLD, reduced adipocyte hypertrophy and dysfunction can trigger lipolysis, increasing circulating NEFA (non-esterified fatty acid) levels. Excess NEFAs are taken up by the liver, where they are re-esterified to TG or oxidized; when oxidation and export capacity are limited, TG accumulates. Chronic lipolysis also increases VLDL-TG production and secretion, which can worsen steatosis if clearance is impaired. Human studies link elevated circulating NEFA, reduced adiponectin, and increased inflammatory/adipokine signals (e.g., PAI-1) with hepatic fat accumulation and progression to NASH.

Key mechanistic points:
- Adipose inflammation and insulin resistance reduce adipocyte TG storage and increase lipolysis, elevating hepatic FFA load.
- Increased VLDL secretion from both hepatic DNL and adipose-derived FFAs contributes to IHTG, especially when LDL receptor–mediated uptake or ketone body flux is low.

# Biomarkers in Humans

1) Reflecting DNL:
- Fasting insulin, HOMA-IR, and HbA1c index insulin resistance, a driver of hepatic fat synthesis.
- Liver fat by MRI/MRS and hepatic steatosis on ultrasound are direct measures of IHTG burden.
- Serum alanine aminotransferase (ALT/AST) and gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) reflect hepatocellular injury and steatosis.
- Indirect proxies of lipogenesis include elevated VLDL-TG secretion or low HDL-C; however, these are less specific to DNL than direct imaging or liver fat estimates.

2) Reflecting Adipose Lipolysis:
- Circulating NEFA (free fatty acids) after fasting and during oral glucose/insulin tolerance tests reflect adipose lipolysis and splanchnic extraction.
- Adiponectin (high-molecular-weight adipokine) inversely correlates with insulin resistance and lipolysis; low levels associate with steatosis.
- Adipokine markers of inflammation such as PAI-1 (plasminogen activator inhibitor-1) and TNF-α are elevated in NAFLD and correlate with IHTG and NASH severity.
- Subcutaneous and visceral adipose tissue thickness and echointensity by imaging reflect adipocyte dysfunction and lipolysis propensity.

3) Integrated flux biomarkers:
- Stable isotope tracer studies (e.g., [1-13C]palmitate or [2H5]glucose) can partition hepatic TG between endogenous (DNL) and exogenous (dietary/adipose-derived) sources; these are considered the gold standard but are invasive and less accessible.
- Fasting acetylcarnitine and malonyl-CoA can reflect mitochondrial oxidation and ACC activity, respectively, offering insight into the balance between lipogenesis and oxidation.

# Clinical Takeaways

- DNL primarily drives IHTG when the liver is exposed to excess carbohydrates and when insulin action is preserved in hepatocytes; adipose lipolysis primarily drives IHTG when FFAs are chronically elevated and export capacity (VLDL and LDL receptor-mediated) is limited.
- In NAFLD, both pathways often act synergistically: insulin resistance increases DNL while suppressing adipocyte storage, thereby increasing lipolysis and NEFA delivery to the liver.
- Best human biomarkers:
  - For DNL: imaging-based hepatic fat (MRI/MRS), HOMA-IR/insulin levels, and, where feasible, stable isotope-based flux partitioning.
  - For adipose lipolysis: fasting and post-challenge NEFA, adiponectin, and inflammatory adipokines (PAI-1/TNF-α), with imaging of adipose tissue morphology to infer dysfunction.

# Evidence Gaps and Future Directions

Human studies frequently rely on indirect biomarkers due to the invasiveness and cost of direct flux measurements. Longitudinal interventional studies that combine diet modification (carbohydrate restriction), insulin sensitizers, and adipokine modulation will clarify how to preferentially target each pathway in NAFLD subtypes.
