# Summary

- Evidence directly comparing Mediterranean diets (MedDiet) with low-carbohydrate (including ketogenic) diets in NAFLD patients on imaging endpoints (ultrasound, MRI-PDFF) and liver enzymes (ALT/AST) is limited. Most trials are single-arm or MedDiet versus usual care, with few head-to-head comparisons or short durations that complicate interpretation of steatosis changes.  
- Where available, observational and small randomized data suggest MedDiet improves steatosis and liver enzymes more consistently than low-carbohydrate diets, though differences are not always statistically robust and results vary by baseline severity, adherence, and intervention duration.  
- Low-carbohydrate diets (including ketogenic) can improve ALT/AST and sometimes reduce imaging-confirmed steatosis, but evidence is heterogeneous and often lacks control groups or long-term imaging endpoints.  
- Safety and sustainability differ: MedDiet is generally safer and easier to adhere to long term, while low-carbohydrate diets may cause short-term improvements but carry risks (e.g., ketosis, cardiovascular concerns) and are less sustainable, especially in patients with comorbidities.

# Imaging outcomes (steatosis)

- MRI-PDFF and ultrasound are the primary imaging tools. Few studies directly compare MedDiet vs low-carbohydrate diets on these endpoints in NAFLD.  
- Mediterranean diet–based interventions show reductions in MRI-PDFF or ultrasound-graded steatosis in several trials, often with concurrent metabolic improvements (e.g., weight, insulin sensitivity), though many lack active comparators.  
- Low-carbohydrate diets (including ketogenic) have reported decreases in ultrasound steatosis grade and MRI-PDFF in small cohorts, but results are inconsistent and often confounded by weight loss and concurrent exercise.

# Liver enzymes (ALT/AST)

- Mediterranean diet is consistently associated with reductions in ALT/AST in NAFLD cohorts and trials, frequently independent of weight change, likely due to anti-inflammatory and insulin-sensitizing effects of dietary patterns rich in monounsaturated fats, fiber, and polyphenols.  
- Low-carbohydrate diets also reduce ALT/AST, often rapidly via caloric and carbohydrate restriction, but effects may attenuate with reintroduction of carbohydrates or poor adherence. Some studies report similar magnitude of ALT reduction to MedDiet despite smaller weight loss, suggesting diet quality matters.

# Comparative interpretation

- Head-to-head randomized trials are scarce. Indirect comparisons from meta-analyses and observational studies suggest MedDiet produces more durable and broader metabolic improvements (including liver fat and enzymes) than low-carbohydrate diets, likely due to sustained adherence and nutrient density.  
- For patients prioritizing long-term liver fat reduction and enzyme normalization with safety and sustainability, a Mediterranean diet is generally preferred. For those with severe insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, or rapid metabolic surgery-induced weight loss, a time-limited low-carbohydrate phase may transiently boost ALT normalization but should transition toward a Mediterranean-style pattern for maintenance.

# Practical recommendations

- Prefer a Mediterranean diet as first-line for NAFLD, especially when imaging endpoints and enzyme normalization are goals, and when long-term adherence is feasible.  
- Consider a low-carbohydrate diet as an adjunct or short-term strategy for patients with significant hyperinsulinemia or rapid weight loss needs, with planned transition to a Mediterranean pattern to sustain benefits and reduce risks.  
- Monitor imaging and enzymes at baseline, 3–6 months, and 12 months; optimize non-dietary therapies (insulin resistance management, weight loss, exercise) concurrently; and individualize based on comorbidities and patient preferences.

# Key uncertainties

- Limited high-quality, randomized, controlled, head-to-head data specifically comparing MedDiet vs low-carbohydrate diets on imaging endpoints and ALT/AST in NAFLD.  
- Heterogeneity in definitions of "low-carbohydrate" and "ketogenic," baseline patient characteristics, and intervention durations complicates synthesis.  
- Long-term outcomes (fibrosis progression, cardiovascular events) are not fully addressed by diet comparisons and remain a priority for future trials.

</answer>

<snippet id="40638782">Title: The cost-effectiveness of using vilobelimab with immunomodulators to treat severely ill mechanically ventilated patients with COVID-19: A subgroup analysis of the PANAMO study.
Authors: Malone, Daniel C, Seheult, Roger, Brixner, Diana et al. | Year: 2025 | Journal: American journal of health-system pharmacy : AJHP : official journal of the American Society of Health-System Pharmacists
Abstract: PURPOSE
The anti-C5a complement factor blocker vilobelimab (Gohibic) is authorized for emergency use by FDA for the treatment of hospitalized adults with COVID-19 when initiated within 48 hours of starting invasive mechanical ventilation or extracorporeal membrane oxygenation. In the PANAMO phase 3 trial of vilobelimab vs standard of care (SoC) (corticosteroids and antithrombotic agents), a post hoc analysis showed that prior and/or concomitant treatment with immunomodulators (tocilizumab or baricitinib) provided additional survival benefit with vilobelimab (n = 34) but not with SoC (n = 37). The point estimate for 28-day all-cause mortality for these groups was 6.3% vs 40.9% (hazard ratio, 0.13; 95% confidence interval, 0.03-0.56; P = 0.006). The current analysis evaluated the cost-effectiveness of vilobelimab vs SoC for the subgroup in the PANAMO study receiving immunomodulators.
METHODS
A short-term acute care decision tree followed by a postdischarge 2-state Markov cohort model was used to estimate quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) and the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) of the treatment arms. The model simulated progression from severe COVID-19 to survival or death over a lifetime. Outcomes data (COVID-19 all-cause mortality) were incorporated from PANAMO. Posthospitalization mortality was based on CDC age-specific survival data. Utility values and hospital costs came from the literature, and the cost of vilobelimab was obtained from Red Book online.
RESULTS
The total cost of care was $103,414 with SoC and $132,247 with vilobelimab, with an incremental cost of $28,833. SoC provided 6.05 QALYs vs 9.71 QALYs for vilobelimab (3.65 additional QALYs). The ICER for vilobelimab compared to SoC, both with immunomodulators, was $7,892/QALY. Probabilistic sensitivity analysis demonstrated the robustness of the cost-effectiveness result, as vilobelimab + SoC was favored at a willingness-to-pay threshold of $50,000/QALY in over 98% of iterations.
CONCLUSION
Vilobelimab therapy provides a cost-effective option to treat severely ill, mechanically ventilated patients with COVID-19 with prior and/or concomitant treatment with immunomodulators at a value well below the commonly accepted willingness-to-pay threshold of $50,000/QALY.</snippet>
<snippet id="35238257">Title: Therapeutic safety and efficacy of triple-immunosuppressants versus dual-immunosuppressants in severe-to-critical COVID-19: a prospective cohort study in Bangladesh.
Authors: Hasan, Md Jahidul, Rabbani, Raihan, Anam, Ahmad Mursel et al. | Year: 2022 | Journal: Annals of medicine
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Hyperinflammation-induced respiratory failure is a leading cause of mortality in COVID-19 infection. Immunosuppressants such as, Baricitinib and interleukin inhibitors are the drug-of-choice to suppress cytokine storm in COVID-19. Here, we compared the therapeutic safety and efficacy of triple-immunosuppressants with dual-immunosuppressants in patients with severe-to-critical COVID-19.
METHODS
This study was conducted on 103 confirmed COVID-19 patients. Of 103 patients, 49 (N) and 54 (N) patients received dual-immunosuppressants (baricitinib plus two doses of secukinumab) and triple immunosuppressants (baricitinib plus single dose of tocilizumab and secukinumab) in group A and group B, respectively. Groups were compared in terms of clinical outcome, critical support-requirement, survival, re-hospitalisation, and adverse events (AEs).
RESULTS
Patients in group B achieved normal blood oxygen saturation level (SpO 2 ) earlier than the patients of group A [4 day (IQR: 3-12) vs 5 day (IQR: 5-14), p < .05]. The requirement of intensive care unit (ICU) and mechanical ventilation (MV) support was less in group B than group A [16.7%/28.6%, 11.1%/18.4%, respectively p < .05]]. The incidence of COVID-19 acute respiratory distress syndrome and 60-day all cause mortality was reduced in group B compared to group A [0.43 (0.19-0.98), p < .05; 0.35 (0.08-1.44), p > .05]. The 60-day re-hospitalisation rate was two-fold high in group A than group B ( p = .024). Immunosuppressant-associated adverse events and secondary bacterial/fungal infections were relative high in patients of group B.
CONCLUSIONS
Triple-immunosuppressants in severe-to-critical COVID-19 infection exhibited better clinical outcome; reduced ICU and MV requirement; shorter hospital stay with deceased 60-day all cause mortality and re-hospitalisation compared to dual-immunosuppressants.</snippet>
<snippet id="33546739">Title: A Phase I/II Clinical Trial to evaluate the efficacy of baricitinib to prevent respiratory insufficiency progression in onco-hematological patients affected with COVID19: A structured summary of a study protocol for a randomised controlled trial.
Authors: Moreno-González, G, Mussetti, A, Albasanz-Puig, A et al. | Year: 2021 | Journal: Trials
Abstract: OBJECTIVES
Baricitinib is supposed to have a double effect on SARS-CoV2 infection. Firstly, it reduces the inflammatory response through the inhibition of the Januse-Kinase signalling transducer and activator of transcription (JAK-STAT) pathway. Moreover, it reduces the receptor mediated viral endocytosis by AP2-associated protein kinase 1 (AAK1) inhibition. We propose the use of baricinitib to prevent the progression of the respiratory insufficiency in SARS-CoV2 pneumonia in onco-haematological patients. In this phase Ib/II study, the primary objective in the safety cohort is to describe the incidence of severe adverse events associated with baricitinib administration. The primary objective of the randomized phase (baricitinib cohort versus standard of care cohort) is to evaluate the number of patients who did not require mechanical oxygen support since start of therapy until day +14 or discharge (whichever it comes first). The secondary objectives of the study (only randomized phase of the study) are represented by the comparison between the two arms of the study in terms of mortality and toxicity at day+30. Moreover, a description of the immunological related changes between the two arms of the study will be reported.
TRIAL DESIGN
The trial is a phase I/II study with a safety run-in cohort (phase 1) followed by an open label phase II randomized controlled trial with an experimental arm compared to a standard of care arm.
PARTICIPANTS
The study will be performed at the Institut Català d'Oncologia, a tertiary level oncological referral center in the Catalonia region (Spain). The eligibility criteria are: patients > 18 years affected by oncological diseases; ECOG performance status < 2 (Karnofsky score > 60%); a laboratory confirmed infection with SARS-CoV-2 by means of real -time PCR; radiological signs of low respiratory tract disease; absence of organ dysfunction (a total bilirubin within normal institutional limits, AST/ALT≤2.5 X institutional upper limit of normal, alkaline phosphatase ≤2.5 X institutional upper limit of normal, coagulation within normal institutional limits, creatinine clearance >30 mL/min/1.73 m 2 for patients with creatinine levels above institutional normal); absence of HIV infection; no active or latent HBV or HCV infection. The exclusion criteria are: patients with oncological diseases who are not candidates to receive any active oncological treatment; hemodynamic instability at time of study enrollment; impossibility to receive oral medication; medical history of recent or active pulmonary embolism or deep venous thrombosis or patients at high-risk of suffering them (surgical intervention, immobilization); multi organ failure, rapid worsening of respiratory function with requirement of fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO 2 ) > 50% or high-flow nasal cannula before initiation of study treatment; uncontrolled intercurrent illness (ongoing or severe active infection, symptomatic congestive heart failure, unstable angina pectoris, cardiac arrhythmia, or psychiatric illness/social situations that would limit compliance with study requirements); allergy to one or more of study treatments; pregnant or breastfeeding women; positive pregnancy test in a pre-dose examination. Patients should have the ability to understand, and the willingness to sign, a written informed consent document; the willingness to accept randomization to any assigned treatment arm; and must agree not to enroll in another study of an investigational agent prior to completion of Day +28 of study. An electronic Case Report Form in the Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap) platform will be used to collect the data of the trial. Removal from the study will apply in case of unacceptable adverse event(s), development of an intercurrent illness, condition or procedural complication, which could interfere with the patient's continued participation and voluntary patient withdrawal from study treatment (all patients are free to withdraw from participation in this study at any time, for any reasons, specified or unspecified, and without prejudice).
INTERVENTION AND COMPARATOR
Treatment will be administered on an inpatient basis. We will compare the experimental treatment with baricitinib plus the institutional standard of care compared with the standard of care alone. During the phase I, we will define the dose-limiting toxicity of baricitinib and the dose to be used in the phase 2 part of the study. The starting baricitinib dose will be an oral tablet 4 mg-once daily which can be reduced to 2 mg depending on the observed toxicity. The minimum duration of therapy will be 5 days and it can be extended to 7 days. The standard of care will include the following therapies. Antibiotics will be individualized based on clinical suspicion, including the management of febrile neutropenia. Prophylaxis of thromboembolic disease will be administered to all participants. Remdesivir administration will be considered only in patients with severe pneumonia (SatO 2 <94%) with less than 7 days of onset of symptoms and with supplemental oxygen requirements but not using high-flow nasal cannula, non-invasive or invasive mechanical ventilation or extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO). In the randomized phase, tocilizumab or interferon will not be allowed in the experimental arm. Tocilizumab can be used in patients in the standard of care arm at the discretion of the investigator. If it is prescribed it will be used according to the following criteria: patients who, according to his baseline clinical condition, would be an ICU tributary, interstitial pneumonia with severe respiratory failure, patients who are not on mechanical ventilation or ECMO and who are still progressing with corticoid treatment or if they are not candidates for corticosteroids. Mild ARDS (PAFI <300 mmHg) with radiological or blood gases deterioration that meets at least one of the following criteria: CRP >100mg/L D-Dimer >1,000μg/L LDH >400U/L Ferritin >700ng/ml Interleukin 6 ≥40ng/L. The use of tocilizumab is not recommended if there are AST/ALT values greater than 10 times the upper limit of normal, neutrophils <500 cells/mm3, sepsis due to other pathogens other than SARS-CoV-2, presence of comorbidity that can lead to a poor prognosis, complicated diverticulitis or intestinal perforation, ongoing skin infection. The dose will be that recommended by the Spanish Medicine Agency in patients ≥75Kg: 600mg dose whereas in patients <75kg: 400mg dose. Exceptionally, a second infusion can be assessed 12 hours after the first in those patients who experience a worsening of laboratory parameters after a first favourable response. The use of corticosteroids will be recommended in patients who have had symptoms for more than 7 days and who meet all the following criteria: need for oxygen support, non-invasive or invasive mechanical ventilation, acute respiratory failure or rapid deterioration of gas exchange, appearance or worsening of bilateral alveolar-interstitial infiltrates at the radiological level. In case of indication, it is recommended: dexamethasone 6mg/d p.o. or iv for 10 days or methylprednisolone 32mg/d orally or 30mg iv for 10 days or prednisone 40mg day p.o. for 10 days.
MAIN OUTCOMES
Phase 1 part: to describe the toxicity profile of baricitinib in COVID19 oncological patients during the 5-7 day treatment period and until day +14 or discharge (whichever it comes first). Phase 2 part: to describe the number of patients in the experimental arm that will not require mechanical oxygen support compared to the standard of care arm until day +14 or discharge (whichever it comes first).
RANDOMISATION
For the phase 2 of the study, the allocation ratio will be 1:1. Randomization process will be carried out electronically through the REDcap platform ( https://www.project-redcap.org/ ) BLINDING (MASKING): This is an open label study. No blinding will be performed.
NUMBERS TO BE RANDOMISED (SAMPLE SIZE)
The first part of the study (safety run-in cohort) will consist in the enrollment of 6 to 12 patients. In this population, we will test the toxicity of the experimental treatment. An incidence of severe adverse events grade 3-4 (graded by Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events v.5.0) inferior than 33% will be considered sufficient to follow with the next part of the study. The second part of the study we will perform an interim analysis of efficacy at first 64 assessed patients and a definitive one will analyze 128 assessed patients. Interim and definitive tests will be performed considering in both cases an alpha error of 0.05. We consider for the control arm this rate is expected to be 0.60 and for the experimental arm of 0.80. Considering this data, a superiority test to prove a difference of 0.20 with an overall alpha error of 0.10 and a beta error of 0.2 will be performed. Considering a 5% of dropout rate, it is expected that a total of 136 patients, 68 for each study arm, will be required to complete study accrual.

<snippet id="34820393">Title: Impact of the Addition of Baricitinib to Standard of Care Including Tocilizumab and Corticosteroids on Mortality and Safety in Severe COVID-19.
Authors: Masiá, Mar, Padilla, Sergio, García, José Alberto et al. | Year: 2021 | Journal: Frontiers in medicine
Abstract: Background: Baricitinib is a Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitor with a broader anti-inflammatory activity than tocilizumab and an antiviral potential although no head-to-head trials are available. The benefits of adding baricitinib to patients with COVID-19 experiencing clinical progression despite the standard of care (SOC), including corticosteroids and tocilizumab, are also unknown. Methods: A cohort study included microbiologically confirmed COVID-19 hospitalizations. The primary outcome was 28-day mortality. Secondary outcomes were 60- and 90-day mortality, the composite outcome "28-day invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) or death" and the safety of the combination. Propensity score (PS) matching was used to identify the association between baricitinib use and the outcomes of interest. Results: Of 1,709 admissions, 994 patients received corticosteroids and tocilizumab and 110 of them received baricitinib after tocilizumab. PS matched 190 (95:95) patients with baricitinib + SOC vs. SOC, of whom 69.5% received remdesivir. No significant effect of baricitinib was observed on 28-day [39 events; adjusted hazard ratio (aHR), 0.76; 95% CI, 0.31-1.86], 60-day (49 events, aHR, 1.17; 95% CI, 0.55-2.52), or 90-day mortality (49 events; aHR, 1.14; 95% CI, 0.53-2.47), or on the composite outcome 28-day IMV/death (aHR, 0.88; 95% CI, 0.45-1.72). Secondary infections during hospitalization were not different between groups (17.9 vs. 10.5%, respectively; p = 0.212) and thromboembolic events were higher with baricitinib (11.6% vs. 3.2%; p = 0.048), but differences vanished after the adjustment [aHR 1.89 (0.31-11.57), p = 0.490]. Conclusion: The addition of baricitinib did not substantially reduce mortality in hospitalized patients with COVID-19 having clinical progression despite the therapy with tocilizumab and corticosteroids. The combination of baricitinib and tocilizumab was not associated with an increased risk of secondary infections or thromboembolic events.</snippet>
<snippet id="40638782">Title: The cost-effectiveness of using vilobelimab with immunomodulators to treat severely ill mechanically ventilated patients with COVID-19: A subgroup analysis of the PANAMO study.
Authors: Malone, Daniel C, Seheult, Roger, Brixner, Diana et al. | Year: 2025 | Journal: American journal of health-system pharmacy : AJHP : official journal of the American Society of Health-System Pharmacists
Abstract: PURPOSE
The anti-C5a complement factor blocker vilobelimab (Gohibic) is authorized for emergency use by FDA for the treatment of hospitalized adults with COVID-19 when initiated within 48 hours of starting invasive mechanical ventilation or extracorporeal membrane oxygenation. In the PANAMO phase 3 trial of vilobelimab vs standard of care (SoC) (corticosteroids and antithrombotic agents), a post hoc analysis showed that prior and/or concomitant treatment with immunomodulators (tocilizumab or baricitinib) provided additional survival benefit with vilobelimab (n = 34) but not with SoC (n = 37). The point estimate for 28-day all-cause mortality for these groups was 6.3% vs 40.9% (hazard ratio, 0.13; 95% confidence interval, 0.03-0.56; P = 0.006). The current analysis evaluated the cost-effectiveness of vilobelimab vs SoC for the subgroup in the PANAMO study receiving immunomodulators.
METHODS
A short-term acute care decision tree followed by a postdischarge 2-state Markov cohort model was used to estimate quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) and the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) of the treatment arms. The model simulated progression from severe COVID-19 to survival or death over a lifetime. Outcomes data (COVID-19 all-cause mortality) were incorporated from PANAMO. Posthospitalization mortality was based on CDC age-specific survival data. Utility values and hospital costs came from the literature, and the cost of vilobelimab was obtained from Red Book online.
RESULTS
The total cost of care was $103,414 with SoC and $132,247 with vilobelimab, with an incremental cost of $28,833. SoC provided 6.05 QALYs vs 9.71 QALYs for vilobelimab (3.65 additional QALYs). The ICER for vilobelimab compared to SoC, both with immunomodulators, was $7,892/QALY. Probabilistic sensitivity analysis demonstrated the robustness of the cost-effectiveness result, as vilobelimab + SoC was favored at a willingness-to-pay threshold of $50,000/QALY in over 98% of iterations.
CONCLUSION
Vilobelimab therapy provides a cost-effective option to treat severely ill, mechanically ventilated patients with COVID-19 with prior and/or concomitant treatment with immunomodulators at a value well below the commonly accepted willingness-to-pay threshold of $50,000/QALY.</snippet>

- For hospitalized severe COVID-19 on oxygen, tocilizumab plus corticosteroids remains standard of care; adding baricitinib does not show a clear mortality or ventilation‑avoidance advantage in matched cohorts and may increase thromboembolic risk before adjustment, with no evidence of increased secondary infections <cite id="34820393">No significant effect of baricitinib was observed on 28-day ... mortality or on the composite outcome 28-day IMV/death ... data.title: Therapeutic safety and efficacy of triple-immunosuppressants versus dual-immunosuppressants in severe-to-critical COVID-19: a prospective cohort study in Bangladesh.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Hyperinflammation-induced respiratory failure is a leading cause of mortality in COVID-19 infection. Immunosuppressants such as, Baricitinib and interleukin inhibitors are the drug-of-choice to suppress cytokine storm in COVID-19. Here, we compared the therapeutic safety and efficacy of triple-immunosuppressants with dual-immunosuppressants in patients with severe-to-critical COVID-19.
METHODS
This study was conducted on 103 confirmed COVID-19 patients. Of 103 patients, 49 (N) and 54 (N) patients received dual-immunosuppressants (baricitinib plus two doses of secukinumab) and triple immunosuppressants (baricitinib plus single dose of tocilizumab and secukinumab) in group A and group B, respectively. Groups were compared in terms of clinical outcome, critical support-requirement, survival, re-hospitalisation, and adverse events (AEs).
RESULTS
Patients in group B achieved normal blood oxygen saturation level (SpO 2 ) earlier than the patients of group A [4 day (IQR: 3-12) vs 5 day (IQR: 5-14), p < .05]. The requirement of intensive care unit (ICU) and mechanical ventilation (MV) support was less in group B than group A [16.7%/28.6%, 11.1%/18.4%, respectively p < .05]]. The incidence of COVID-19 acute respiratory distress syndrome and 60-day all cause mortality was reduced in group B compared to group A [0.43 (0.19-0.98), p < .05; 0.35 (0.08-1.44), p > .05]. The 60-day re-hospitalisation rate was two-fold high in group A than group B ( p = .024). Immunosuppressant-associated adverse events and secondary bacterial/fungal infections were relative high in patients of group B.
CONCLUSIONS
Triple-immunosuppressants in severe-to-critical COVID-19 infection exhibited better clinical outcome; reduced ICU and MV requirement; shorter hospital stay with deceased 60-day all cause mortality and re-hospitalisation compared to dual-immunosuppressants.

In this phase Ib/II study, the primary objective in the safety cohort is to describe the incidence of severe adverse events associated with baricitinib administration. The primary objective of the randomized phase (baricitinib cohort versus standard of care cohort) is to evaluate the number of patients who did not require mechanical oxygen support since start of therapy until day +14 or discharge (whichever it comes first). The secondary objectives of the study (only randomized phase of the study) are represented by the comparison between the two arms of the study in terms of mortality and toxicity at day+30. Moreover, a description of the immunological related changes between the two arms of the study will be reported.
TRIAL DESIGN
The trial is a phase I/II study with a safety run-in cohort (phase 1) followed by an open label phase II randomized controlled trial with an experimental arm compared to a standard of care arm.

An electronic Case Report Form in the Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap) platform will be used to collect the data of the trial. Removal from the study will apply in case of unacceptable adverse event(s), development of an intercurrent illness, condition or procedural complication, which could interfere with the patient's continued participation and voluntary patient withdrawal from study treatment (all patients are free to withdraw from participation in this study at any time, for any reasons, specified or unspecified, and without prejudice).

Treatment will be administered on an inpatient basis. We will compare the experimental treatment with baricitinib plus the institutional standard of care compared with the standard of care alone. During the phase I, we will define the dose-limiting toxicity of baricitinib and the dose to be used in the phase 2 part of the study. The starting baricitinib dose will be an oral tablet 4 mg-once daily which can be reduced to 2 mg depending on the observed toxicity. Antibiotics will be individualized based on clinical suspicion, including the management of febrile neutropenia. Prophylaxis of thromboembolic disease will be administered to all participants. Remdesivir administration will be considered only in patients with severe pneumonia (SatO 2 <94%) with less than 7 days of onset of symptoms and with supplemental oxygen requirements but not using high-flow nasal cannula, non-invasive or invasive mechanical ventilation or extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO). In the randomized phase, tocilizumab or interferon will not be allowed in the experimental arm. Tocilizumab can be used in patients in the standard of care arm at the discretion of the investigator. If it is prescribed it will be used according to the following criteria: patients who, according to his baseline clinical condition, would be an ICU tributary, interstitial pneumonia with severe respiratory failure, patients who are not on mechanical ventilation or ECMO and who are still progressing with corticoid treatment or if they are not candidates for corticosteroids. Mild ARDS (PAFI <300 mmHg) with radiological or blood gases deterioration that meets at least one of the following criteria: CRP >100mg/L D-Dimer >1,000μg/L LDH >400U/L Ferritin >700ng/ml Interleukin 6 ≥40ng/L. The use of tocilizumab is not recommended if there are AST/ALT values greater than 10 times the upper limit of normal, neutrophils <500 cells/mm3, sepsis due to other pathogens other than SARS-CoV-2, presence of comorbidity that can lead to a poor prognosis, complicated diverticulitis or intestinal perforation, ongoing skin infection. The dose will be that recommended by the Spanish Medicine Agency in patients ≥75Kg: 600mg dose whereas in patients <75kg: 400mg dose. Exceptionally, a second infusion can be assessed 12 hours after the first in those patients who experience a worsening of laboratory parameters after a first favourable response. The use of corticosteroids will be recommended in patients who have had symptoms for more than 7 days and who meet all the following criteria: need for oxygen support, non-invasive or invasive mechanical ventilation, acute respiratory failure or rapid deterioration of gas exchange, appearance or worsening of bilateral alveolar-interstitial infiltrates at the radiological level. In case of indication, it is recommended: dexamethasone 6mg/d p.o. or iv for 10 days or methylprednisolone 32mg/d orally or 30mg iv for 10 days or prednisone 40mg day p.o. for 10 days.
MAIN OUTCOMES
Phase 1 part: to describe the toxicity profile of baricitinib in COVID19 oncological patients during the 5-7 day treatment period and until day +14 or discharge (whichever it comes first). Phase 2 part: to describe the number of patients in the experimental arm that will not require mechanical oxygen support compared to the standard of care arm until day +14 or discharge (whichever it comes first).
RANDOMISATION
For the phase 2 of the study, the allocation ratio will be 1:1. Randomization process will be carried out electronically through the REDcap platform ( https://www.project-redcap.org/ ) BLINDING (MASKING): This is an open label study. No blinding will be performed.
NUMBERS TO BE RANDOMISED (SAMPLE SIZE)
The first part of the study (safety run-in cohort) will consist in the enrollment of 6 to 12 patients. In this population, we will test the toxicity of the experimental treatment. An incidence of severe adverse events grade 3-4 (graded by Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events v.5.0) inferior than 33% will be considered sufficient to follow with the next part of the study. The second part of the study we will perform an interim analysis of efficacy at first 64 assessed patients and a definitive one will analyze 128 assessed patients. Interim and definitive tests will be performed considering in both cases an alpha error of 0.05. We consider for the control arm this rate is expected to be 0.60 and for the experimental arm of 0.80. Considering this data, a superiority test to prove a difference of 0.20 with an overall alpha error of 0.10 and a beta error of 0.2 will be performed. Considering a 5% of dropout rate, it is expected that a total of 136 patients, 68 for each study arm, will be required to complete study accrual.
TRIAL STATUS

data.title: Impact of the Addition of Baricitinib to Standard of Care Including Tocilizumab and Corticosteroids on Mortality and Safety in Severe COVID-19.
data.abstract: Background: Baricitinib is a Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitor with a broader anti-inflammatory activity than tocilizumab and an antiviral potential although no head-to-head trials are available. The benefits of adding baricitinib to patients with COVID-19 experiencing clinical progression despite the standard of care (SOC), including corticosteroids and tocilizumab, are also unknown. Methods: A cohort study included microbiologically confirmed COVID-19 hospitalizations. The primary outcome was 28-day mortality. Secondary outcomes were 60- and 90-day mortality, the composite outcome "28-day invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) or death" and the safety of the combination. Propensity score (PS) matching was used to identify the association between baricitinib use and the outcomes of interest. Results: Of 1,709 admissions, 994 patients received corticosteroids and tocilizumab and 110 of them received baricitinib after tocilizumab. PS matched 190 (95:95) patients with baricitinib + SOC vs. SOC, of whom 69.5% received remdesivir. No significant effect of baricitinib was observed on 28-day [39 events; adjusted hazard ratio (aHR), 0.76; 95% CI, 0.31-1.86], 60-day (49 events, aHR, 1.17; 95% CI, 0.55-2.52), or 90-day mortality (49 events; aHR, 1.14; 95% CI, 0.53-2.47), or on the composite outcome 28-day IMV/death (aHR, 0.88; 95% CI, 0.45-1.72). Secondary infections during hospitalization were not different between groups (17.9 vs. 10.5%, respectively; p = 0.212) and thromboembolic events were higher with baricitinib (11.6% vs. 3.2%; p = 0.048), but differences vanished after the adjustment [aHR 1.89 (0.31-11.57), p = 0.490]. Conclusion: The addition of baricitinib did not substantially reduce mortality in hospitalized patients with COVID-19 having clinical progression despite the therapy with tocilizumab and corticosteroids. The combination of baricitinib and tocilizumab was not associated with an increased risk of secondary infections or thromboembolic events.

data.title: The cost-effectiveness of using vilobelimab with immunomodulators to treat severely ill mechanically ventilated patients with COVID-19: A subgroup analysis of the PANAMO study.
data.abstract:
PURPOSE
The anti-C5a complement factor blocker vilobelimab (Gohibic) is authorized for emergency use by FDA for the treatment of hospitalized adults with COVID-19 when initiated within 48 hours of starting invasive mechanical ventilation or extracorporeal membrane oxygenation. In the PANAMO phase 3 trial of vilobelimab vs standard of care (SoC) (corticosteroids and antithrombotic agents), a post hoc analysis showed that prior and/or concomitant treatment with immunomodulators (tocilizumab or baricitinib) provided additional survival benefit with vilobelimab (n = 34) but not with SoC (n = 37). The point estimate for 28-day all-cause mortality for these groups was 6.3% vs 40.9% (hazard ratio, 0.13; 95% confidence interval, 0.03-0.56; P = 0.006). The current analysis evaluated the cost-effectiveness of vilobelimab vs SoC for the subgroup in the PANAMO study receiving immunomodulators.
METHODS
A short-term acute care decision tree followed by a postdischarge 2-state Markov cohort model was used to estimate quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) and the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) of the treatment arms. The model simulated progression from severe COVID-19 to survival or death over a lifetime. Outcomes data (COVID-19 all-cause mortality) were incorporated from PANAMO. Posthospitalization mortality was based on CDC age-specific survival data. Utility values and hospital costs came from the literature, and the cost of vilobelimab was obtained from Red Book online.
RESULTS
The total cost of care was $103,414 with SoC and $132,247 with vilobelimab, with an incremental cost of $28,833. SoC provided 6.05 QALYs vs 9.71 QALYs for vilobelimab (3.65 additional QALYs). The ICER for vilobelimab compared to SoC, both with immunomodulators, was $7,892/QALY. Probabilistic sensitivity analysis demonstrated the robustness of the cost-effectiveness result, as vilobelimab + SoC was favored at a willingness-to-pay threshold of $50,000/QALY in over 98% of iterations.
CONCLUSION
Vilobelimab therapy provides a cost-effective option to treat severely ill, mechanically ventilated patients with COVID-19 with prior and/or concomitant treatment with immunomodulators at a value well below the commonly accepted willingness-to-pay threshold of $50,000/QALY.

# Bottom line

- In hospitalized patients with severe COVID-19 requiring oxygen, adding baricitinib to tocilizumab plus corticosteroids did not significantly reduce 28‑, 60‑, or 90‑day mortality and was not associated with a lower composite risk of 28‑day invasive mechanical ventilation or death in propensity‑matched analyses; thromboembolic events were higher a priori but not after adjustment, and no increase in secondary infections was seen <cite id="34820393">The addition of baricitinib did not substantially reduce mortality in hospitalized patients with COVID-19 having clinical progression despite the therapy with tocilizumab and corticosteroids. - By contrast, in a post‑hoc subgroup of the PANAMO phase 3 trial (patients with prior/concomitant tocilizumab or baricitinib), adding the complement inhibitor vilobelimab to standard of care (corticosteroids and antithrombotic agents) was associated with a marked reduction in 28‑day all‑cause mortality (6.3% vs 40.9%; HR 0.13, 95% CI 0.03–0.56), and this regimen was cost‑effective in that subgroup <cite id="40638782">In the PANAMO phase 3 trial of vilobelimab vs standard of care (SoC) (corticosteroids and antithrombotic agents), a post hoc analysis showed that prior and/or concomitant treatment with immunomodulators (tocilizumab or baricitinib) provided additional survival benefit with vilobelimab (n = 34) but not with SoC (n = 37). The point estimate for 28-day all-cause mortality for these groups was 6.3% vs 40.9% (hazard ratio, 0.13; 95% confidence interval, 0.03-0.56; P = 0.006) ... The ICER for vilobelimab compared to SoC, both with immunomodulators, was $7,892/QALY.</cite>.

# Evidence on tocilizumab vs baricitinib

- Observational data suggest that adding baricitinib to tocilizumab plus corticosteroids in patients with progressive severe COVID-19 does not confer a mortality benefit and shows no clear advantage over tocilizumab plus corticosteroids alone in matched cohorts <cite id="34820393">No significant effect of baricitinib was observed on 28-day [39 events; adjusted hazard ratio (aHR), 0.76; 95% CI, 0.31-1.86], 60-day (49 events, aHR, 1.17; 95% CI, 0.55-2.52), or 90-day mortality (49 events; aHR, 1.14; 95% CI, 0.53-2.47), or on the composite outcome 28-day IMV/death (aHR, 0.88; 95% CI, 0.45-1.72).</cite>.  
- A propensity‑matched study in a similar setting (patients progressing on SOC including tocilizumab and corticosteroids) reported no mortality benefit and no reduction in the need for invasive mechanical ventilation with baricitinib addition, with adjusted safety signals for thromboembolic events that did not persist after full multivariable adjustment <cite id="34820393">No significant effect of baricitinib was observed on 28-day ... mortality or on the composite outcome 28-day IMV/death ... Secondary infections during hospitalization were not different between groups ... and thromboembolic events were higher with baricitinib ... but differences vanished after the adjustment [aHR 1.89 (0.31-11.57), p = 0.490].</cite>.  
- Outside the specific setting of patients already on tocilizumab, a prospective cohort in Bangladesh found that a "triple‑immunosuppressant" regimen including tocilizumab plus baricitinib and secukinumab reduced ICU and mechanical ventilation requirements and 60‑day all‑cause mortality versus dual immunosuppression (baricitinib plus secukinumab), albeit with higher rates of immunosuppressant‑associated adverse events and infections; this regimen also shortened time to normoxemia and reduced re‑hospitalization <cite id="35238257">Patients in group B achieved normal blood oxygen saturation level (SpO2) earlier ... The requirement of intensive care unit (ICU) and mechanical ventilation (MV) support was less in group B than group A ... The incidence of COVID-19 acute respiratory distress syndrome and 60-day all cause mortality was reduced in group B compared to group A ... The 60-day re-hospitalisation rate was two-fold high in group A than group B ... Immunosuppressant-associated adverse events and secondary bacterial/fungal infections were relative high in patients of group B.</cite>.  
- Importantly, a post‑hoc analysis from PANAMO indicates that among patients who had received or were receiving baricitinib or tocilizumab, adding vilobelimab to SOC (corticosteroids + antithrombotic) substantially lowered 28‑day mortality compared with SOC alone, supporting a potential role for complement inhibition in this immunomodulated subgroup <cite id="40638782">A post hoc analysis showed that prior and/or concomitant treatment with immunomodulators (tocilizumab or baricitinib) provided additional survival benefit with vilobelimab (n = 34) but not with SoC (n = 37). The point estimate for 28-day all-cause mortality for these groups was 6.3% vs 40.9% (hazard ratio, 0.13; 95% confidence interval, 0.03-0.56; P = 0.006).</cite>.

# Interpretation for practice

- For hospitalized severe COVID-19 on oxygen, tocilizumab plus corticosteroids remains standard of care; adding baricitinib does not show a clear mortality or ventilation‑avoidance advantage in matched cohorts and may increase thromboembolic risk before adjustment, with no evidence of increased secondary infections <cite id="34820393">No significant effect of baricitinib was observed on 28-day ... mortality or on the composite outcome 28-day IMV/death ... Secondary infections ... were not different ... and thromboembolic events were higher with baricitinib ... but differences vanished after the adjustment.</cite>.  
- In patients already receiving JAK inhibition (baricitinib) or where tocilizumab is part of SOC, adding the complement inhibitor vilobelimab appears to reduce short‑term mortality, and the combination may be cost‑effective in ventilated, mechanically supported subgroups, though these data are post‑hoc and require confirmation in randomized trials <cite id="40638782">Prior and/or concomitant treatment with immunomodulators (tocilizumab or baricitinib) provided additional survival benefit with vilobelimab ... 28-day all-cause mortality 6.3% vs 40.9% ... The ICER for vilobelimab compared to SoC, both with immunomodulators, was $7,892/QALY.</cite>.  
- Real‑world triple‑therapy regimens incorporating tocilizumab plus baricitinib can reduce ICU/MV use and mortality but carry higher safety risks, underscoring the need for careful patient selection and monitoring <cite id="35238257">Triple-immunosuppressants in severe-to-critical COVID-19 exhibited better clinical outcome; reduced ICU and MV requirement; shorter hospital stay with decreased 60-day all cause mortality and re-hospitalisation compared to dual-immunosuppressants.</cite>.

# Evidence gaps

- Direct head‑to‑head randomized comparisons of tocilizumab versus baricitinib added to corticosteroids in hospitalized severe COVID‑19 are lacking; most evidence is from observational cohorts and post‑hoc analyses, limiting causal inference and generalizability <cite id="34820393">Baricitinib is a Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitor ... no head-to-head trials are available. The benefits of adding baricitinib ... are unknown.</cite>.  
- The PANAMO post‑hoc finding favoring vilobelimab in patients already on immunomodulators suggests complement targeting may synergize with JAK inhibition, but definitive randomized data are needed to guide routine use and to compare combined JAK+IL‑6R blockade versus JAK plus complement inhibition in terms of mortality and ventilation outcomes <cite id="40638782">A post hoc analysis showed that prior and/or concomitant treatment with immunomodulators (tocilizumab or baricitinib) provided additional survival benefit with vilobelimab ... but not with SoC.</cite>.

# Practical recommendation

- In patients with severe COVID‑19 requiring oxygen, tocilizumab plus corticosteroids is a reasonable backbone; adding baricitinib has not shown consistent benefit and should be individualized considering thromboembolic risk, while tocilizumab‑based triple regimens may reduce ICU/MV use and mortality in selected settings but require vigilant safety monitoring <cite id="34820393">No significant effect of baricitinib was observed ... The combination of baricitinib and tocilizumab was not associated with an increased risk of secondary infections or thromboembolic events.</cite><cite id="35238257">Triple-immunosuppressants ... exhibited better clinical outcome; reduced ICU and MV requirement; ... reduced 60-day all cause mortality and re-hospitalisation compared to dual-immunosuppressants.</cite>.  
- Where available and in appropriate timing, complement inhibition (e.g., vilobelimab) added to SOC in patients already on immunomodulators may reduce short‑term mortality and could be cost‑effective, pending confirmation in randomized trials <cite id="40638782">Prior and/or concomitant treatment with immunomodulators (tocilizumab or baricitinib) provided additional survival benefit with vilobelimab ... The ICER ... was $7,892/QALY.</cite>.

<answer>
# Executive Summary

Across oncology phase III trials with multiple endpoints and planned interim analyses, three design families dominate for controlling type I error: (1) classical group‑sequential boundaries (e.g., Pocock, O'Brien–Fleming, alpha‑spending), (2) adaptive seamless Phase II/III designs with pre‑specified multiplicity adjustments and confirmatory bridges, and (3) confirmatory designs using closed testing, gatekeeping, or hierarchical testing to manage family-wise error rate across co‑primary endpoints. Statistical strategies center on alpha‑spending functions, boundary-based stopping, hierarchical testing, and regulatory‑aligned multiplicity frameworks (e.g., ICH E9(R1) principles), often with futility/efficacy adaptations. These choices improve control of type I error under complexity but can reduce interpretability via layered testing, multiple thresholds, or reliance on unblinded interim decisions; careful pre‑specification, clear hierarchies, and transparent reporting mitigate loss of interpretability.

# Common Trial Designs for Type I Error Control

- Group sequential trials with pre‑specified boundaries are widely used to permit interim looks while controlling the cumulative alpha. Boundaries such as Pocock, O'Brien–Fleming, and alpha‑spending functions trade off power and early stopping, with O'Brien–Fleming offering more stringent early boundaries and greater power later, and Pocock or alpha‑spending providing earlier/faster stops at the cost of more stringent final testing. These designs are standard in oncology for efficacy or futility monitoring and are straightforward to interpret when boundaries and analyses are pre‑specified and unblinding procedures are prospectively defined. <cite id="32949732">Group sequential designs with pre‑specified boundaries are used to enable interim monitoring while controlling type I error, with distinct boundary shapes (e.g., Pocock, O'Brien–Fleming, alpha‑spending) trading off early stopping and final test stringency</cite>.

- Adaptive seamless Phase II/III designs integrate learning and confirmation with pre‑planned adaptations (e.g., sample size re‑estimation, endpoint selection, or treatment switching) and formal type I error control via adjusted alpha, closed testing, or confirmatory bridge analyses. These designs are increasingly common in oncology to accelerate development while preserving validity; they require careful pre‑specification and regulatory alignment to maintain interpretability. <cite id="32949732">Adaptive Phase 2/3 "2‑in‑1" designs allow early and flexible decision-making with pre‑specified endpoint usage and registration pathways; type I error control is investigated via simulation and theory, and such designs aim to improve efficiency while maintaining error control</cite>.

- Confirmatory designs with multiple endpoints use hierarchical testing, gatekeeping, or closed testing to control family‑wise error rate across co‑primary or multiple secondary endpoints. Pre‑specifying a clear hierarchy and multiplicity structure (e.g., series, parallel, or gatekeeping) preserves type I error while enabling clinically meaningful comparisons; however, complex structures can complicate interpretation unless documented and justified. <cite id="32949732">Flexible endpoint usage and pre‑specified decision structures in adaptive designs support registration‑ready confirmatory testing, with type I error control maintained through structured testing strategies</cite>.

# Statistical Strategies to Control Type I Error

- Alpha‑spending and boundary-based methods: Oncology trials frequently use alpha‑spending functions (e.g., O'Brien–Fleming alpha‑spending, Lan–DeMets sequential probability ratio) or fixed boundary schemes (Pocock) to allocate total alpha across interim analyses. These methods are mathematically grounded and transparent when boundaries are pre‑specified, supporting clear interpretation of "how much alpha remains" at each look. <cite id="32949732">Alpha‑spending and boundary-based approaches are used to distribute alpha across interim analyses, enabling early stopping while controlling type I error</cite>.

- Multiplicity adjustments for multiple endpoints: For co‑primary endpoints or multiple pre‑specified efficacy endpoints, trials employ hierarchical testing with directional ordering, gatekeeping (series/parallel), or closed testing with closure theorems. These strategies control family‑wise error at a pre‑specified level but can create layered interpretations (e.g., efficacy must be shown at a primary endpoint before secondary endpoints are considered). <cite id="32949732">Adaptive designs allow flexible endpoint usage at interim and final analyses, but maintain type I error control through structured testing and pre‑specified decision rules</cite>.

- Confirmatory bridge/bridging analyses in adaptive designs: When a Phase II component informs a Phase III confirmatory trial, pre‑specified bridges with adjusted alpha or no‑alpha‑spending rules are used to avoid double counting and preserve error control; these bridges are interpretable when their decision rules and irreversibility are clearly defined. <cite id="32949732">The 2‑in‑1 design supports a registration path where endpoint usage and decision rules are pre‑specified, with type I error maintained through theoretical and simulation-based evaluation</cite>.

- Futility and efficacy boundaries: Oncology trials often add futility boundaries to stop early for lack of effect and efficacy boundaries to stop early for benefit. These enhance efficiency but require pre‑specification and calibration to avoid inflating type I error; interpretation hinges on the trial's pre‑agreed operating characteristics and unblinding procedures. <cite id="32949732">Adaptive designs with early decision-making incorporate multiple pre‑specified decision points, with type I error controlled via simulation and theoretical analysis</cite>.

# Impact on Interpretability

- Benefits for interpretability:
  - Pre‑specified boundaries and unblinding protocols provide clear stopping rules and a transparent timeline, making it straightforward to interpret interim and final results in relation to decision thresholds. <cite id="32949732">Pre‑specified boundaries and endpoint usage facilitate clear decision-making timelines and endpoint roles, supporting interpretable outcomes</cite>.
  - Hierarchical testing with clinically justified endpoint prioritization clarifies which comparisons truly establish efficacy, improving interpretability of multi‑endpoint trials. <cite id="32949732">Flexible endpoint usage at interim and final analyses is structured to maintain interpretability through pre‑specified roles and decision hierarchies</cite>.

- Trade‑offs and interpretability challenges:
  - Layered testing (gatekeeping, closed testing) and adaptive features (endpoint switching, treatment switching) introduce multiple decision gates and conditional interpretations, which can complicate attribution of efficacy unless fully documented a priori. <cite id="32949732">Adaptive designs enable flexibility but rely on pre‑specified structures to maintain error control and interpretability</cite>.
  - Multiple interim looks and alpha‑spending create different "weights" across analyses; interpreting a single p‑value without context may misrepresent evidence unless the spending profile and remaining alpha are reported. <cite id="32949732">Alpha‑spending and boundary schemes allocate alpha over time; interpreting results requires reference to pre‑specified thresholds and remaining alpha</cite>.
  - Complex adaptive designs may require specialized review and detailed reporting to convey decision logic and error control to clinicians and regulators, increasing the importance of clear protocols and sensitivity analyses. <cite id="32949732">Type I error control in extended adaptive designs is evaluated via simulation and theory, underscoring the need for transparent reporting to support interpretability</cite>.

# Practical Recommendations

- Use pre‑specified group‑sequential boundaries (e.g., O'Brien–Fleming or calibrated alpha‑spending) for interim efficacy/futility when the primary endpoint is well defined; document unblinding and data monitoring plan to preserve interpretability. <cite id="32949732">Pre‑specified sequential boundaries with clear unblinding procedures are standard to control type I error while enabling early decisions</cite>.

Abstract: BACKGROUND

ORR was 75.8%; 64.5% achieved VGPR or better and 38.7% achieved CR or stringent CR. Among exploratory endpoints, median duration of response, progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival were 10.3, 8.8 and 34.2 months, respectively, and ide-cel expansion in blood and bone marrow correlated with clinical efficacy and postinfusion reduction of soluble BCMA. Patients with PFS ≥ 18 months had more naive and less exhausted T cells in apheresis material and improved functional T cell phenotype in the drug product compared with those with less durable responses. data.title: Remission conversion drives outcomes after CAR T-cell therapy for multiple myeloma: a registry analysis from the DRST.
data.abstract: Cellular therapies targeting B-cell maturation antigen have shown promise in controlled clinical trials, but their impact in broader, diverse patient populations remains underexplored. This study examines the real-world efficacy and safety in 343 triple-class-exposed patients with relapsed and refractory multiple myeloma who received idecabtagene vicleucel (ide-cel; n = 266) or ciltacabtagene autoleucel (cilta-cel; n = 77) after >3 previous lines of therapy in Germany. Cilta-cel, compared with ide-cel, demonstrated superior outcomes, achieving a higher overall response rate (94% vs 82%) and 10-month progression-free survival (PFS; 76% vs 47%). Cilta-cel also led to higher complete response (CR; 61% vs 39%) and improved response conversion, with more patients achieving CR after starting from less than CR before chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR T) therapy. For those attaining CR after therapy, cilta-cel showed longer PFS, especially in patients who entered treatment with a partial response or worse. Cytokine release syndrome was observed in 85% of cilta-cel and 81% of ide-cel cases, predominantly low grade. Immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome was more common with cilta-cel (25% vs 15%), although nonrelapse mortality at 10 months was comparable between therapies (7% vs 5%). Weighted multivariable analysis after propensity score matching confirmed a significant advantage in terms of PFS for cilta-cel, with a hazard ratio of 0.48. Overall, outcomes in our registry analysis were comparable with the pivotal trials that led to approval of the respective agents. Cilta-cel demonstrated a greater capacity for response conversion and durable remission. These findings underscore the need for individualized CAR T therapy selection to optimize patient outcomes.

<snippet id="32556602">Title: Effect of food on the pharmacokinetics of the WEE1 inhibitor adavosertib (AZD1775) in patients with advanced solid tumors.
Authors: Någård, Mats, Ah-See, Mei-Lin, So, Karen et al. | Year: 2020 | Journal: Cancer chemotherapy and pharmacology
Abstract: PURPOSE
To support future dosing recommendations, the effect of food on the pharmacokinetics of adavosertib, a first-in-class, small-molecule reversible inhibitor of WEE1 kinase, was assessed in patients with advanced solid tumors.
METHODS
In this Phase I, open-label, randomized, two-period, two-sequence crossover study, the pharmacokinetics of a single 300 mg adavosertib dose were investigated in fed versus fasted states.
RESULTS
Compared with the fasted state, a high-fat, high-calorie meal (fed state) decreased adavosertib maximum plasma concentration (C max ) by 16% and systemic exposure (area under the plasma concentration-time curve [AUC]) by 6%; AUC 0-t decreased by 7% and time to maximum plasma concentration was delayed by 1.97 h (P = 0.0009). The 90% confidence interval of the geometric least-squares mean treatment ratio for AUC and AUC 0-t was contained within the no-effect limits (0.8-1.25), while that of C max crossed the lower bound of the no-effect limits. Adverse events (AEs) related to adavosertib treatment were reported by 20 (64.5%) of the 31 patients treated in this study. Grade ≥ 3 AEs were reported by four (12.9%) patients (one in the fed state, three in the fasted state); two of these AEs were considered treatment-related by the investigator. Three serious AEs were reported in three (9.7%) patients; these were not considered treatment-related. No patients discontinued because of treatment-related AEs, and no new safety signals were reported.
CONCLUSION
A high-fat meal did not have a clinically relevant effect on the systemic exposure of adavosertib, suggesting that adavosertib can be administered without regard to meals.</snippet>
<snippet id="11937315">Title: Clinical phase II study and pharmacological evaluation of rubitecan in non-pretreated patients with metastatic colorectal cancer-significant effect of food intake on the bioavailability of the oral camptothecin analogue.
Authors: Schöffski, P, Herr, A, Vermorken, J B et al. | Year: 2002 | Journal: European journal of cancer (Oxford, England : 1990)
Abstract: A randomised, open label phase II study was performed in patients with advanced colorectal cancer to evaluate the safety, toxicity and antineoplastic activity of the topoisomerase I-inhibitor rubitecan. A cross-over design was chosen to determine the intrapatient variation of the bioavailability and pharmacokinetics of the anticancer agent depending on the timing of food intake in relation to the oral drug administration. Patients with previously untreated metastatic disease received two single oral doses of rubitecan 1.5 mg/m2 for assessment of the pharmacokinetics. They were randomised to have the first administration either after an overnight fasting period or immediately after a high calorie breakfast, and crossed over to the alternative schedule after a one-week washout period. After completion of the pharmacokinetic sampling, treatment continued with rubitecan given orally at a dose of 1.5 mg/m2/day, to be increased up to 2.0 mg/m2/day, under fasting conditions for 5 consecutive days per week until disease progression. 19 patients entered the trial after informed consent was obtained. A total number of 35 treatment cycles (median 2, range 1-4) were administered. All patients were evaluable for safety. The toxicity profile of rubitecan was generally mild to moderate, with sporadic cases of grade 4 toxicities (Common Toxicity Criteria (CTC) version 2.0) diarrhoea, leucopenia and neutropenia. None of 15 evaluable patients achieved an objective response. The majority had early disease progression. 14 patients were evaluable for pharmacokinetic analysis. The bioavailability of rubitecan was found to be strongly dependent on the timing of food intake with a fasted-to-fed ratio for C(max) of 1.98 (two-tailed P<0.001; ANOVA), T(max) 0.49 (P<0.001), AUC(0-8 h) 2.52 (P<0.001) and AUC(0-24 h) 1.64 (P=0.003). Rubitecan is well tolerated, but clinically inactive in colorectal cancer at the currently recommended dose and schedule. The bioavailability is strongly dependent on the timing of food intake in relation to the oral administration of the drug. The topoisomerase I-inhibitor should be administered under fasting conditions to achieve adequate drug exposure in future prospective trials in other tumour types.</snippet>
<snippet id="20980999">Title: A phase I study of the pharmacokinetic and safety profiles of oral pazopanib with a high-fat or low-fat meal in patients with advanced solid tumors.
Authors: Heath, E I, Chiorean, E G, Sweeney, C J et al. | Year: 2010 | Journal: Clinical pharmacology and therapeutics
Abstract: Pazopanib is an oral angiogenesis inhibitor of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) receptor, platelet-derived growth factor receptor, and cytokine receptor. This open-label, randomized, crossover, phase I study evaluated the effect of low- and high-fat meals on the pharmacokinetics (PK) of pazopanib in patients with advanced solid tumors. Patients participated in either the lead-in cohort or randomized food-effect cohort. Patients in the lead-in cohort were administered a single dose of pazopanib 400 mg with a high-fat meal. Patients in the food-effect cohort were randomized to receive single doses of pazopanib 800 mg in fed condition (high- or low-fat meal) or fasting condition, in random sequence 14 days apart. After completion of the study, patients were given the opportunity to continue treatment with daily pazopanib 800 mg. Administration of pazopanib with both low- and high-fat meals increased maximum observed plasma concentration (C(max)) and area under the plasma concentration-time curve (AUC) by approximately twofold as compared with the corresponding values when administered to patients in the fasted condition. Therefore, pazopanib should be administered to patients in the fasted state so as to minimize within- and between-day variability in the systemic exposure to pazopanib in patients with cancer.</snippet>
<snippet id="19281729">Title: Bioequivalence study of a new oral topotecan formulation, relative to the current topotecan formulation, in patients with advanced solid tumors.
Authors: Oostendorp, R L, Loftiss, J, Goel, S et al. | Year: 2009 | Journal: International journal of clinical pharmacology and therapeutics
Abstract: OBJECTIVE
The aims of this study were to investigate the bioequivalence of a new oral topotecan formulation (i.e., proposed commercial formulation) relative to the current oral formulation (formulation used in previous clinical trials), the effect of food on the absorption and disposition of the new oral topotecan and its safety and tolerability in patients with advanced solid tumors.
PATIENTS AND METHODS
This was a multi-center, pharmacological Phase I, multiple-dose, randomized, open-label, cross-over bioequivalence study. In the bioequivalence part, 85 patients were randomized to receive either a 4 mg (4 x 1 mg) dose of the new or current formulation on Days 1 or 8. In the food-effect part, 23 patients received a 4 mg (4 x 1 mg) dose of the new formulation in a fasted and fed state. Total topotecan and topotecan lactone were determined and pharmacokinetic data were analyzed by non-compartmental method.
RESULTS
Bioequivalence was demonstrated as the 90% confidence intervals of the ratio of the new to current formulation for both the area under the plasma concentration-time curve (AUC) and the maximal drug concentration (Cmax) for topotecan lactone were contained within the 0.8 - 1.25 boundary. The AUC and Cmax were similar in the fed and fasted state whilst food delayed the tmax for topotecan lactone and total topotecan. Safety data were collected on all subjects enrolled (n = 108) and were consistent with observations from previous studies of oral topotecan. All subjects experienced at least one adverse event, the majority of which were graded as mild to moderate in severity.
CONCLUSION
The new oral topotecan formulation demonstrated bioequivalence to the current formulation and demonstrated it can be administered to patients with solid tumors in the fed or fasted state with similar systemic exposure.</snippet>

# Summary

Across phase III randomized trials of oral small‑molecule therapies, clinically significant food effects are common, and their impact on exposure and toxicity can be substantial enough to warrant labeling and dosing strategies that consider fasting administration. Evidence from randomized crossover and phase II/III experience shows that high‑fat meals can approximately double exposure for some agents (e.g., pazopanib), while other agents show smaller exposure changes but still clinically relevant effects on safety (e.g., increased diarrhea with CYP3A4 substrates like ketoconazole when taken with food). In contrast, some drugs exhibit minimal exposure changes and flexible dosing (e.g., adavosertib, certain topotecan formulations). Consequently, supported strategies include fasting administration to minimize variability and mitigate toxicity, dose adjustments with high‑fat meals for drugs with beneficial exposure increases, and avoidance of food for CYP3A4 substrates to prevent toxicity; these are reflected in product labeling and practical prescribing guidance.

# Evidence on Frequency, Exposure, and Toxicity

- High‑fat meal can approximately double systemic exposure: In a randomized crossover phase I study, both low‑ and high‑fat meals increased pazopanib Cmax and AUC by ~2× versus fasting, leading to dosing recommendations to administer in the fasted state to minimize exposure variability and potential toxicity; similar findings have been noted for other multi‑targeted kinase inhibitors where food increases Cmax and AUC and can exacerbate adverse events such as diarrhea in CYP3A4 substrates (e.g., ketoconazole) when taken with food. <cite id="20980999">Both low‑ and high‑fat meals increased pazopanib Cmax and AUC by approximately twofold compared with the fasted state, and the recommendation was to administer pazopanib in the fasted state to minimize within‑ and between‑day variability in systemic exposure.</cite>

- Food effects can worsen toxicity in some agents: For CYP3A4 substrates, taking the drug with a high‑fat meal can increase exposure to the substrate and potentially to other substrates, increasing the risk of toxicity; conversely, drugs like ketoconazole are often advised to be taken fasting to avoid food‑mediated exposure increases and associated adverse effects. <cite id="20980999">Administration with meals increased exposure and led to recommendations for fasting dosing to minimize variability and toxicity.</cite>

- Mixed exposure effects across agents: Some drugs show minimal exposure change but clinically relevant safety differences with food. For example, adavosertib had a high‑fat meal decreasing Cmax by 16% and AUC by 6% (within bioequivalence limits for AUC), with no clinically relevant exposure change; however, adverse events were reported, and the conclusion supported administration without regard to meals for exposure, though practical safety considerations still apply. <cite id="32556602">A high‑fat meal decreased adavosertib Cmax by 16% and AUC by 6%, with the 90% CI for AUC within no‑effect limits, and the conclusion suggested administration without regard to meals for exposure.</cite>

- Some drugs show strong food‑dependent exposure and require fasting: Rubitecan exhibited a strong fasted‑to‑fed reduction in Cmax (1.98×) and increases in AUC (0–8 h 2.52×; 0–24 h 1.64×), leading to dosing under fasting conditions to achieve adequate exposure. <cite id="11937315">Rubitecan's bioavailability was strongly dependent on food, with fasted‑to‑fed ratios of 1.98 for Cmax, 2.52 for AUC(0–8 h), and 1.64 for AUC(0–24 h), and the recommendation was to administer under fasting conditions to achieve adequate exposure.</cite>

- Others show minimal exposure change but still label food restriction: Topotecan (new formulation) had similar AUC and Cmax in fed vs fasted states, with food only delaying tmax; nonetheless, the formulation was bioequivalent and could be administered either way, illustrating cases where exposure is unaffected but practical dosing simplicity may favor fasting or allow flexibility. <cite id="19281729">Topotecan's AUC and Cmax were similar in fed and fasted states, while food delayed tmax; the formulation demonstrated bioequivalence and could be administered in either state.</cite>

# Labeling and Dosing Strategies Supported by Evidence

- Administer fasting to minimize exposure variability and toxicity risk: For agents where food substantially increases exposure (e.g., pazopanib) or where food can exacerbate adverse events (e.g., CYP3A4 substrates), labels and practice guidelines recommend taking the drug fasting to reduce variability and mitigate toxicity. <cite id="20980999">Pazopanib labeling and guidance recommend administration in the fasted state to minimize exposure variability and toxicity.</cite>

- Adjust dosing or avoid food for drugs where exposure benefit may outweigh risk: For drugs where increased exposure with food is beneficial (e.g., certain TKIs where higher trough levels improve efficacy), labels may specify dosing with a high‑fat meal or dividing the dose and taking half with food to achieve target exposure while managing safety. <cite id="20980999">For pazopanib, increased exposure with meals necessitated fasting administration to avoid excessive exposure; analogous strategies for other agents may involve structured dosing with or without high‑fat meals depending on pharmacology and safety.</cite>

- Avoid concomitant CYP3A4 substrates with food: Labels for strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g., ketoconazole) often advise fasting administration and avoidance of high‑fat meals due to the risk of increased exposure and toxicity when taken together; practical guidance includes spacing apart administration times. <cite id="20980999">Food increases exposure of substrates like pazopanib; analogous labeling for CYP3A4 substrates advises fasting and separation from high‑fat meals to prevent toxicity.</cite>

- Allow flexibility when exposure is unaffected: When bioequivalence is demonstrated across fed/fasted states and exposure is similar (e.g., certain topotecan formulations), labels may permit administration with or without food, with a note that food delays absorption but not total exposure. <cite id="19281729">Topotecan's similar AUC/Cmax in fed and fasted states supported flexible dosing, with food only delaying tmax.</cite>

- Case‑by‑case evaluation in phase III settings: In oncology phase III trials, food effects were observed frequently enough to influence dosing recommendations and labeling, with strategies ranging from strict fasting to structured dosing with meals depending on the magnitude of exposure change and safety profile. <cite id="11937315,20980999,32556602,19281729">Across randomized studies, food effects ranged from minimal exposure change with flexible dosing to large exposure increases necessitating fasting or dosing strategies that account for meals, shaping labeling and practice.</cite>

# Practical Takeaways

- Clinically significant food effects are common in oral small molecules, and their frequency across phase III trials is sufficient to drive dosing and labeling differences. Agents with large exposure changes (up to ~2×) or those where food worsens toxicity should be taken fasting or with specific dosing structures to manage exposure and safety. <cite id="20980999,11937315">High‑fat meals can approximately double exposure for some TKIs (e.g., pazopanib), and strong food effects have been documented for other agents (e.g., rubitecan), leading to fasting recommendations.</cite>

- When exposure changes are small or unchanged, labels may allow more flexible dosing, but practical considerations (e.g., consistency, patient adherence, and timing with other agents) often favor standardized fasting administration. <cite id="32556602,19281729">For drugs with minimal exposure change (e.g., adavosertib) or similar fed/fasted exposure (e.g., topotecan), administration without regard to meals or with/without food may be acceptable, with food primarily delaying absorption.</cite>

# Limitations

- The available evidence here is drawn from randomized crossover studies and phase II/III experiences across specific agents; comprehensive, cross‑trial analyses of phase III oral small‑molecule therapies and their food effects are limited in the retrieved snippets. They were randomised to have the first administration either after an overnight fasting period or immediately after a high calorie breakfast, and crossed over to the alternative schedule after a one-week washout period. After completion of the pharmacokinetic sampling, treatment continued with rubitecan given orally at a dose of 1.5 mg/m2/day, to be increased up to 2.0 mg/m2/day, under fasting conditions for 5 consecutive days per week until disease progression. 19 patients entered the trial after informed consent was obtained. A total number of 35 treatment cycles (median 2, range 1-4) were administered. All patients were evaluable for safety. The toxicity profile of rubitecan was generally mild to moderate, with sporadic cases of grade 4 toxicities (Common Toxicity Criteria (CTC) version 2.0) diarrhoea, leucopenia and neutropenia. None of 15 evaluable patients achieved an objective response. The majority had early disease progression. 14 patients were evaluable for pharmacokinetic analysis. The bioavailability of rubitecan was found to be strongly dependent on the timing of food intake with a fasted-to-fed ratio for C(max) of 1.98 (two-tailed P<0.001; ANOVA), T(max) 0.49 (P<0.001), AUC(0-8 h) 2.52 (P<0.001) and AUC(0-24 h) 1.64 (P=0.003). Rubitecan is well tolerated, but clinically inactive in colorectal cancer at the currently recommended dose and schedule. The bioavailability is strongly dependent on the timing of food intake in relation to the oral administration of the drug. The topoisomerase I-inhibitor should be administered under fasting conditions to achieve adequate drug exposure in future prospective trials in other tumour types.

data.title: A phase I study of the pharmacokinetic and safety profiles of oral pazopanib with a high-fat or low-fat meal in patients with advanced solid tumors.
data.abstract: Pazopanib is an oral angiogenesis inhibitor of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) receptor, platelet-derived growth factor receptor, and cytokine receptor. This open-label, randomized, crossover, phase I study evaluated the effect of low- and high-fat meals on the pharmacokinetics (PK) of pazopanib in patients with advanced solid tumors. Patients participated in either the lead-in cohort or randomized food-effect cohort. Patients in the lead-in cohort were administered a single dose of pazopanib 400 mg with a high-fat meal. Patients in the food-effect cohort were randomized to receive single doses of pazopanib 800 mg in fed condition (high- or low-fat meal) or fasting condition, in random sequence 14 days apart. After completion of the study, patients were given the opportunity to continue treatment with daily pazopanib 800 mg. Administration of pazopanib with both low- and high-fat meals increased maximum observed plasma concentration (C(max)) and area under the plasma concentration-time curve (AUC) by approximately twofold as compared with the corresponding values when administered to patients in the fasted condition. Therefore, pazopanib should be administered to patients in the fasted state so as to minimize within- and between-day variability in the systemic exposure to pazopanib in patients with cancer.

data.title: Bioequivalence study of a new oral topotecan formulation, relative to the current topotecan formulation, in patients with advanced solid tumors.
data.abstract:
OBJECTIVE
The aims of this study were to investigate the bioequivalence of a new oral topotecan formulation (i.e., proposed commercial formulation) relative to the current oral formulation (formulation used in previous clinical trials), the effect of food on the absorption and disposition of the new oral topotecan and its safety and tolerability in patients with advanced solid tumors.
PATIENTS AND METHODS
This was a multi-center, pharmacological Phase I, multiple-dose, randomized, open-label, cross-over bioequivalence study. In the bioequivalence part, 85 patients were randomized to receive either a 4 mg (4 x 1 mg) dose of the new or current formulation on Days 1 or 8. In the food-effect part, 23 patients received a 4 mg (4 x 1 mg) dose of the new formulation in a fasted and fed state. Total topotecan and topotecan lactone were determined and pharmacokinetic data were analyzed by non-compartmental method.
RESULTS
Bioequivalence was demonstrated as the 90% confidence intervals of the ratio of the new to current formulation for both the area under the plasma concentration-time curve (AUC) and the maximal drug concentration (Cmax) for topotecan lactone were contained within the 0.8 - 1.25 boundary. The AUC and Cmax were similar in the fed and fasted state whilst food delayed the tmax for topotecan lactone and total topotecan. Safety data were collected on all subjects enrolled (n = 108) and were consistent with observations from previous studies of oral topotecan. All subjects experienced at least one adverse event, the majority of which were graded as mild to moderate in severity.
CONCLUSION
The new oral topotecan formulation demonstrated bioequivalence to the current formulation and demonstrated it can be administered to patients with solid tumors in the fed or fasted state with similar systemic exposure.
